exercises.title: ACL Rehabilitation Exercises
exercises.summary: ACL rehabilitation exercises after injury or reconstruction. Phases, milestones and return-to-sport criteria from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The knee needs full extension, strong quadriceps and hamstrings, and excellent control before returning to sport. You will often see it in our programmes for ACL tear and meniscal injury, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Phase 1: reduce swelling, regain full straightening, quad activation.
Phase 2: full bend, normal walking, basic strengthening.
Phase 3: progressive strength, balance, single-leg control.
Phase 4: running, jumping and landing training.
Phase 5: sport-specific drills and return-to-sport testing.
exercises.howMuch: Daily exercise with regular supervised sessions.
warnings: The knee gives way, swells after activity or locks.

faqs.q: When can I run again?
faqs.a: Often around 3 to 4 months, if strength and control criteria are met.

faqs.q: Why does return to sport take so long?
faqs.a: The graft and the neuromuscular control both need time. Rushing raises re-injury risk.

exercises.title: Adductor Stretch
exercises.summary: Adductor stretch for groin tightness and hip mobility. Butterfly and side lunge versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stretching the adductors improves hip range for sport, squatting and activities like getting in and out of a car. It is a regular part of rehab plans for hip osteoarthritis, cerebral palsy and genu valgum (knock knees), and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Butterfly: sit with the soles of your feet together and knees falling outwards.
Hold your feet and sit tall, gently lowering knees towards the floor.
Hold 30 seconds.
Side lunge: stand with feet wide apart, bend one knee and shift sideways until you feel a stretch in the straight leg's inner thigh.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds, once a day.
commonMistakes: Pressing the knees down forcefully.
Rounding the back.
warnings: Sharp groin pain suggests a strain or hip joint problem.

faqs.q: Is this useful for children with cerebral palsy?
faqs.a: Adductor stretching is often part of their programme, guided by the physiotherapist.

faqs.q: Can I do it after hip replacement?
faqs.a: Some approaches limit wide positions early on. Ask first.

exercises.title: Ankle Circles
exercises.summary: Ankle circles and ankle alphabet exercises for sprains and stiffness. How to do them and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Early movement limits stiffness and helps pump away swelling. The alphabet version combines all ankle directions in a way that is easy to remember. You will often see it in our programmes for ankle sprain, ankle fracture and ankle dislocation, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit or lie with the leg supported and the foot free to move.
Circles: slowly rotate the foot in large circles, 10 clockwise and 10 anticlockwise.
Alphabet: trace the letters A to Z in the air with your big toe.
Keep the movement at the ankle, not the knee.
exercises.howMuch: 10 circles each way or one alphabet, 3 times a day.
commonMistakes: Moving the whole leg.
Rushing through small movements.
warnings: Pain and swelling increase sharply, or you can't bear any weight after injury.

faqs.q: When can I start after a sprain?
faqs.a: Usually within the first couple of days, within a comfortable range.

faqs.q: Is the alphabet exercise useful for fractures?
faqs.a: Once your surgeon or doctor permits ankle movement.

exercises.title: Ankle Pumps
exercises.summary: Ankle pumps for circulation, swelling and DVT risk after surgery. How often and how to do them, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Each contraction of the calf squeezes blood back towards the heart. Frequent pumping reduces swelling and supports circulation when you are less mobile. Our physiotherapists use it most often for ankle fracture, total knee replacement and total hip replacement, and it features in our post-surgical rehabilitation programmes.
steps: Lie or sit with your legs supported.
Pull your toes and foot up towards you as far as comfortable.
Then point your foot away.
Move smoothly and rhythmically.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 20 pumps every hour while awake after surgery, or during long periods of sitting.
commonMistakes: Moving too little to engage the calf.
warnings: You notice calf pain, warmth, redness or swelling in one leg. Seek medical assessment for possible DVT.

faqs.q: Do ankle pumps prevent blood clots?
faqs.a: They support circulation and are part of prevention, alongside medication and early walking where prescribed.

faqs.q: Can I do these on a long flight?
faqs.a: Yes. They are useful during any long period of sitting.

exercises.title: Back Extension Exercise
exercises.summary: Back extension exercise for spine strength, posture and osteoporosis. Technique, reps and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Strong back extensors hold the spine upright and resist forward rounding. Research in osteoporosis supports extensor strengthening for posture and back pain. It is a regular part of rehab plans for lumbar spondylosis, ankylosing spondylitis and scoliosis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie face down with a pillow under your hips and arms by your sides.
Tuck your chin slightly and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Lift your chest a few centimetres off the floor.
Hold 3 to 5 seconds, then lower slowly.
Progress by placing your hands lightly by your temples.
exercises.howMuch: 8 to 10 repetitions, 2 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Lifting too high and crunching the lower back.
Looking up and straining the neck.
warnings: It causes sharp low back pain or leg symptoms.

faqs.q: Is this the same as McKenzie extension?
faqs.a: No. McKenzie uses the arms to push up with the back relaxed. This one uses the back muscles to lift.

faqs.q: Is it safe with osteoporosis?
faqs.a: Gentle extension strengthening is recommended. Avoid forward-bending sit-ups.

exercises.title: Backward Walking
exercises.summary: Backward walking exercise for balance and knee rehab. How to do it safely, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stepping backwards is needed when opening doors or recovering from a push. Practising improves confidence and control. You will often see it in our programmes for knee osteoarthritis, Parkinson's disease and stroke, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand beside a counter with one hand on it.
Take small steps backwards, landing on the ball of the foot then heel.
Keep an upright posture.
Walk 5 metres, then turn and repeat.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 4 lengths, once a day.
warnings: You have a history of backward falls. Practise only with someone next to you.

faqs.q: Why is backward walking hard in Parkinson's?
faqs.a: Postural reactions can be slower. Guided practice helps.

faqs.q: Can I use a treadmill?
faqs.a: Only under supervision at very slow speeds.

exercises.title: Balance Board Exercises
exercises.summary: Balance board and wobble board exercises for ankle sprains and sports rehab. Progressions and safety tips from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The board moves constantly, forcing rapid ankle and hip corrections that train joint position sense. It is a regular part of rehab plans for ankle sprain, ankle instability and ACL tear, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Place the board next to a wall or counter.
Stand on it with both feet and try to keep the edges off the floor.
Rock slowly forwards and back, then side to side, with control.
Progress to single-leg stance, then add ball catches.
exercises.howMuch: 3 rounds of 30 to 60 seconds, once a day.
warnings: Your ankle gives way repeatedly despite training.

faqs.q: When can I start after a sprain?
faqs.a: When you can balance on one leg on the floor for 30 seconds.

faqs.q: Is a cushion enough?
faqs.a: A folded pillow or foam pad is a good first unstable surface.

exercises.title: Balance Training
exercises.summary: Balance training programme for falls prevention and neurological conditions. What's included and how it progresses, from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Balance depends on strength, vision, inner ear and sensation. Training challenges each system progressively. Our physiotherapists use it most often for Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and stroke, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Static balance: feet together, tandem stance, single leg stand.
Dynamic balance: weight shifting, reaching, turning.
Walking challenges: heel-to-toe, sideways, backwards, head turns.
Add difficulty: eyes closed, soft surfaces, dual tasks like counting.
Always have support within reach.
exercises.howMuch: At least 2 to 3 hours per week in total, spread over several sessions, as recommended for falls prevention.
warnings: You have repeated falls, dizziness or blackouts. These need medical assessment.

faqs.q: How long before balance improves?
faqs.a: Many people notice improvement within 6 to 12 weeks of regular practice.

faqs.q: Is walking enough?
faqs.a: Walking helps fitness but specific balance challenges are needed to reduce falls.

exercises.title: Biceps Stretch
exercises.summary: Biceps stretch for arm and shoulder flexibility. Wall and seated versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The biceps crosses both shoulder and elbow. Stretching it improves elbow straightening and shoulder extension. You will often see it in our programmes for biceps tendonitis and elbow fractures, and it features in our shoulder pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand side-on to a wall and place your palm flat on it behind you at shoulder height, thumb up.
Keeping the elbow straight, slowly turn your body away from the wall.
Feel a stretch in the front of the arm and shoulder.
Hold 30 seconds, switch sides.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 holds, once a day.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbow.
warnings: You feel sharp pain at the front of the shoulder, which may indicate tendon irritation.

faqs.q: Should I stretch biceps tendonitis?
faqs.a: Gently, if it doesn't increase pain. Strengthening is often more useful.

faqs.q: Can I do it seated?
faqs.a: Yes: sit with hands behind you on the floor, fingers pointing back, and slide your bottom forward.

exercises.title: Bird Dog
exercises.summary: Bird dog exercise for back pain and core stability. Correct technique, holds and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Controlling rotation and sway of the trunk while the limbs move is exactly what the back needs for daily tasks. The bird dog trains that control safely. Our physiotherapists use it most often for lumbar spondylosis, disc bulge and spondylolisthesis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Kneel on hands and knees with your back flat and neck long.
Gently brace your tummy.
Slide one leg straight back along the floor, then lift it to hip height.
Once steady, add the opposite arm reaching forward at shoulder height.
Hold 5 seconds without the trunk twisting, then return and swap sides.
exercises.howMuch: 6 to 10 repetitions each side, 2 sets, once a day. Increase hold time to 10 seconds.
commonMistakes: Lifting the leg too high and arching the back.
Letting the hips rotate open.
warnings: Pain increases in the lower back or down the leg.

faqs.q: Can I do bird dogs after spine surgery?
faqs.a: Often yes, as part of later rehab, once your surgeon clears you.

faqs.q: Is it better than planks?
faqs.a: They train different demands. Bird dogs put less compression on the spine and suit early rehab.

faqs.q: What is the bird dog?
faqs.a: The bird dog extends one arm and the opposite leg from hands and knees while keeping the trunk steady.

faqs.q: How is the bird dog performed?
faqs.a: Start on hands and knees with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Keep your back flat, like a table. Gently brace your stomach. Slide one leg straight back along the floor, then lift it to hip height. Keep your hips level. Hold for 5 seconds, return, and repeat with the other leg. When that's steady, add the opposite arm: reach it forward as the leg goes back. Start with 5 to 8 slow repetitions each side and build to 10 with a 10-second hold.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of the bird dog?
faqs.a: It builds core stability and balance, supports lower back pain recovery and improves spinal control. It is often part of rehab for lumbar spondylosis, disc bulge and spondylolisthesis.

faqs.q: Which muscles does the bird dog target?
faqs.a: The erector spinae, multifidus, glutes, deep abdominals and shoulder stabilisers.

exercises.title: Bodyweight Squats
exercises.summary: Bodyweight squat technique for leg strength. Depth, form and common mistakes from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Squatting uses the quadriceps, glutes and hamstrings together. It improves strength in the movements used to sit, stand and pick things up. Our physiotherapists use it most often for knee osteoarthritis, total knee replacement and ACL tear, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder width apart, toes slightly turned out.
Push the hips back and bend the knees, as if sitting on a chair.
Keep your chest up and weight through the heels.
Lower to a comfortable depth, ideally thighs parallel to the floor.
Push through the heels to stand, squeezing the glutes.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, 3 days a week.
commonMistakes: Knees collapsing inwards.
Heels lifting.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom.
warnings: Knee pain increases the next day. Reduce depth.

faqs.q: Should knees go past toes?
faqs.a: It's natural for knees to move forward. Pain determines limits, not a rule.

faqs.q: Can I squat with knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Usually yes, within a comfortable depth.

exercises.title: Calf Raises
exercises.summary: Calf raises (heel raises) for Achilles, plantar fasciitis and balance. Double, single and eccentric versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The calf generates push-off with every step. Progressive calf raises are the core of Achilles tendinopathy rehab and help in heel pain and after ankle injuries. Our physiotherapists use it most often for achilles tendon rupture, plantar fasciitis and ankle sprain, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand holding a counter with feet hip width apart.
Rise up onto the balls of your feet as high as you can.
Pause 1 second, then lower slowly over 3 seconds.
Progress to single-leg raises.
Advanced: do them on a step, lowering the heel below the step level.
exercises.howMuch: 15 repetitions, 3 sets, once a day. For tendon rehab, we set specific loads.
commonMistakes: Rolling out onto the little toe side.
Dropping down quickly.
warnings: Achilles pain is worse the next morning and doesn't settle.

faqs.q: Are heel raises and calf raises the same?
faqs.a: Yes. The names are used interchangeably.

faqs.q: How many single-leg raises should I manage?
faqs.a: Around 20 to 25 is a common target for healthy adults, but it varies with age.

exercises.title: Calf Stretch
exercises.summary: Calf stretch for plantar fasciitis, Achilles pain and tight calves. Straight and bent knee versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The gastrocnemius crosses the knee and the soleus doesn't, so stretching with the knee straight and then bent covers both. You will often see it in our programmes for plantar fasciitis, achilles tendon rupture and ankle fracture, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand facing a wall with hands on it.
Step one foot back, keeping the heel down and toes pointing forward.
Bend the front knee and lean towards the wall until you feel a stretch in the back calf.
Hold 30 seconds.
Then bend the back knee slightly, keeping the heel down, to stretch the lower calf. Hold 30 seconds.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 holds of each version, each leg, twice a day.
commonMistakes: Letting the back heel lift.
Turning the back foot outwards.
warnings: After an Achilles rupture, follow your rehab timeline before stretching.

faqs.q: Does calf stretching help heel pain?
faqs.a: It's commonly included in plantar fasciitis treatment together with strengthening.

faqs.q: Can I stretch on a step?
faqs.a: Yes, by dropping the heel over the edge. It's stronger, so build up carefully.

exercises.title: Cat Cow Stretch
exercises.summary: Cat cow (cat camel) stretch for back stiffness and pain. Step-by-step technique and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The four-point position takes body weight off the spine, so the joints can move with little load. Rhythmic movement reduces stiffness and helps the back muscles relax. You will often see it in our programmes for lumbar spondylosis, ankylosing spondylitis and degenerative disc disease, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Kneel on hands and knees, hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
Breathe out and round your back up towards the ceiling, tucking your chin and tailbone.
Breathe in and slowly let your back dip, lifting your chest and tailbone.
Move slowly within a comfortable range.
exercises.howMuch: 10 slow cycles, once or twice a day. Many people like it first thing in the morning.
commonMistakes: Forcing the arch at the lower back.
Moving too quickly.
warnings: Arching or rounding sends pain into a leg.

faqs.q: What if kneeling hurts my knees?
faqs.a: Put a folded towel or cushion under them.

faqs.q: Is cat camel the same exercise?
faqs.a: Yes. The names are used for the same movement.

faqs.q: What is the cat cow stretch?
faqs.a: The cat cow stretch moves the spine between rounding and arching on hands and knees.

faqs.q: How is the cat cow stretch performed?
faqs.a: Get onto your hands and knees, hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Breathe out and round your back up, tucking your tailbone under and letting your head drop. Breathe in and slowly let your back sag, lifting your tailbone and your gaze a little. Move slowly between the two positions. Do 10 slow cycles.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of the cat cow stretch?
faqs.a: It improves spinal mobility, eases back stiffness and suits early back pain rehab and pregnancy. It is often part of rehab for lumbar spondylosis, ankylosing spondylitis and degenerative disc disease.

faqs.q: Which muscles does the cat cow stretch target?
faqs.a: It mobilises the spine and gently works the back extensors and abdominals.

exercises.title: Cervical Isometric Exercises
exercises.summary: Cervical isometric exercises for neck strength. Four directions, how hard to push and how long to hold, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Muscle strength around the neck protects the joints and discs. Isometrics build that strength at a low, controllable effort and often reduce pain in the process. You will often see it in our programmes for cervical spondylosis, cervical myelopathy and rheumatoid arthritis, and it features in our neck pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit tall with a small chin tuck.
Forward: place your palm on your forehead and press your head gently into it, resisting with your hand so nothing moves.
Backward: clasp your hands behind your head and press back into them.
Sideways: place a hand on the side of your head and press your head into it. Repeat on the other side.
Hold each press for 5 to 10 seconds at about a third of your maximum effort.
exercises.howMuch: 5 holds in each direction, once or twice a day. Increase hold time before increasing effort.
commonMistakes: Pushing too hard. Low effort is enough.
Holding your breath.
Letting the head move.
warnings: Pressing in any direction brings on arm symptoms or headache.

faqs.q: How hard should I push?
faqs.a: Gently, about 30 percent effort. You should be able to breathe and talk normally.

faqs.q: Are these safe after whiplash?
faqs.a: Often yes, once serious injury is excluded. We guide the timing.

faqs.q: What are cervical isometric exercises?
faqs.a: Cervical isometric exercises press the head gently into your hand in different directions without moving the neck, building strength safely.

faqs.q: How are cervical isometric exercises performed?
faqs.a: Forward: place your palm on your forehead and gently push your head into it. Your hand resists so the head stays still. Backward: clasp your hands behind your head and push back into them. Sideways: place a hand on the side of your head above the ear and push into it. Repeat on the other side. Rotation: place your hand at the side of your forehead and try to turn into it.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of cervical isometric exercises?
faqs.a: They strengthen the neck when movement is painful, support recovery after strain and suit early rehab. They are often part of rehab for cervical spondylosis, disc bulge and cervical myelopathy.

faqs.q: Which muscles do cervical isometric exercises target?
faqs.a: The neck flexors, extensors, side benders and rotators, depending on direction.

exercises.title: Cervical Rotation
exercises.summary: Cervical rotation exercise for neck stiffness. How to turn the neck safely, reps and precautions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The upper neck joints do much of the work of turning the head. When they stiffen, reversing the car or checking a blind spot becomes difficult. Gentle, repeated rotation restores range and reduces the protective muscle guarding that builds up with pain. It is a regular part of rehab plans for cervical spondylosis, torticollis and ankylosing spondylitis, and it features in our neck pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit upright with your back supported and shoulders relaxed.
Do a small chin tuck first so the head is balanced over the shoulders.
Slowly turn your head to the right as far as is comfortable, keeping your chin level.
Pause for 2 to 3 seconds, return to the middle, then turn to the left.
If one side is tighter, you can add light overpressure with your hand once it moves freely without pain.
exercises.howMuch: 10 turns each way, 2 to 3 times a day. Move within a range that feels like a mild stretch, not pain.
commonMistakes: Tilting the head or dropping the chin while turning.
Rotating the shoulders and trunk instead of the neck.
Moving quickly or jerking to the end of range.
warnings: Turning brings on dizziness, blurred vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing.
Pain or pins and needles travel down an arm.

faqs.q: Is clicking in the neck a problem?
faqs.a: Painless clicking is common and usually harmless. Grinding with pain or other symptoms should be assessed.

faqs.q: Should I push through stiffness?
faqs.a: Work into mild stretch only. Range improves with repetition, not force.

faqs.q: What is the cervical rotation?
faqs.a: Cervical rotation is turning the head slowly from side to side within a comfortable range to keep the neck mobile.

faqs.q: How is the cervical rotation performed?
faqs.a: Sit upright with your back supported and shoulders relaxed. Do a small chin tuck first so your head is centred. Slowly turn your head to the right as far as is comfortable. Keep your chin level; don't let it drop or tilt. Pause for 2 to 3 seconds, then return to centre. Repeat to the left. Do 10 turns each way, two or three times a day.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of the cervical rotation?
faqs.a: It maintains turning range for driving and daily tasks, eases stiffness and helps recovery from neck strain and spondylosis. It is often part of rehab for cervical spondylosis, torticollis and ankylosing spondylitis.

faqs.q: Which muscles does the cervical rotation target?
faqs.a: The sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, splenius and deep rotator muscles of the neck.

exercises.title: Cervical Side Bending
exercises.summary: Cervical side bending exercise for a stiff neck. Steps, reps and mistakes to avoid, explained by Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Side bending moves the neck in a direction we rarely use in daily life. Regular practice keeps the side muscles and joints supple and complements turning and nodding exercises. It is a regular part of rehab plans for cervical spondylosis and torticollis, and it features in our neck pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit tall with your shoulders level and relaxed.
Keep looking straight ahead and slowly tilt your right ear towards your right shoulder.
Stop when you feel a gentle stretch on the left side of the neck. Don't lift the shoulder to meet the ear.
Hold for 3 to 5 seconds, return to centre, then repeat to the left.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions each side, twice a day.
commonMistakes: Turning the face instead of keeping it forward.
Hitching the shoulder up.
Forcing the stretch with a hand before the movement is comfortable.
warnings: Tilting towards one side sends pain or tingling into that arm. This can point to nerve irritation.

faqs.q: Why does tilting one way cause arm pain?
faqs.a: Tilting towards a painful side narrows the space where nerves leave the neck. That needs assessment rather than more stretching.

faqs.q: Can I combine this with heat?
faqs.a: Yes. A warm pack for 10 minutes beforehand can make it more comfortable.

faqs.q: What is the cervical side bending?
faqs.a: Cervical side bending is gently tilting the ear towards the shoulder to stretch and mobilise the side of the neck.

faqs.q: How is the cervical side bending performed?
faqs.a: Sit tall with your shoulders level and relaxed. Slowly tilt your head to bring your right ear towards your right shoulder. Keep looking straight ahead. Stop at the first point of mild stretch on the left side of the neck. Hold for 5 to 10 seconds. Return to centre and repeat on the other side. Aim for 5 to 10 slow repetitions each side, twice a day.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of the cervical side bending?
faqs.a: It relieves stiffness and tightness on the sides of the neck and improves comfortable movement. It is often part of rehab for cervical spondylosis, torticollis and fibromyalgia syndrome.

faqs.q: Which muscles does the cervical side bending target?
faqs.a: It stretches the upper trapezius, scalenes and levator scapulae on the opposite side.

exercises.title: Chair Exercises
exercises.summary: Chair exercises for seniors: seated leg raises, seated marching and mobility. A safe daily routine from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Regular movement maintains muscle strength, joint mobility and circulation. Seated exercise removes the fear of falling that stops many older adults exercising. It is a regular part of rehab plans for knee osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and Parkinson's disease, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Seated marching: sit tall at the front of a firm chair and lift alternate knees, as if marching, for 30 to 60 seconds.
Seated leg raises: straighten one knee and hold for 3 seconds, then lower. Alternate legs.
Ankle pumps and circles.
Arm raises: lift both arms forward and overhead, then lower.
Trunk turns: arms crossed, turn gently left and right.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions of each, once or twice a day. A 10 to 15 minute routine is enough to start.
warnings: You feel chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness. Stop and seek medical advice.

faqs.q: Is chair exercise enough on its own?
faqs.a: It's a good start. Standing balance work should be added when safe.

faqs.q: What chair should I use?
faqs.a: A sturdy chair without wheels, ideally with armrests.

exercises.title: Chest Mobility Exercises
exercises.summary: Chest mobility exercises for stiff chest wall and breathing. Rotation, side bending and arm movements from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: A stiff chest wall limits lung expansion. Moving the ribs and spine increases breathing capacity. It is a regular part of rehab plans for asthma, ankylosing spondylitis and scoliosis, and it features in our upper back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit upright. Breathe in while lifting both arms overhead; breathe out as they lower.
Side bend: breathe in as you reach one arm over your head to the side, out as you return.
Rotation: arms crossed, breathe in and turn to one side, out as you return.
Move slowly with breathing.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions of each, once or twice a day.
warnings: Chest pain or rib pain increases.

faqs.q: Why is this important in ankylosing spondylitis?
faqs.a: AS can stiffen the joints between ribs and spine, reducing chest expansion.

faqs.q: Can I combine with thoracic extension?
faqs.a: Yes, they complement each other.

exercises.title: Chest Stretch
exercises.summary: Doorway chest stretch for rounded shoulders and posture. Technique and hold times from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Tight pectorals pull the shoulders forward. Stretching them supports upright posture and shoulder blade position. You will often see it in our programmes for shoulder impingement, ankylosing spondylitis and cervical spondylosis, and it features in our upper back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand in a doorway with forearms on the frame, elbows at shoulder height.
Step one foot forward and lean gently through the doorway.
Feel the stretch across the front of the chest.
Hold 30 seconds.
Vary arm height slightly to stretch different parts.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds, 1 to 2 times a day.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back.
Leaning too far into shoulder pain.
warnings: You feel tingling down the arms or pain at the front of the shoulder.

faqs.q: Does this help breathing?
faqs.a: Chest mobility can make breathing feel easier for some people.

faqs.q: How long until posture changes?
faqs.a: Stretching helps, but posture change also needs strength and habit.

exercises.title: Child's Pose
exercises.summary: Child's pose stretch for lower back tension. Technique, variations and precautions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The position bends the spine, opens the hips and lengthens the muscles along the back and sides. Slow breathing in the pose helps muscle guarding settle. It is a regular part of rehab plans for lumbar spondylosis and spinal stenosis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Kneel on the floor with knees hip width apart and big toes touching.
Sit back towards your heels.
Reach your arms forward along the floor and lower your chest towards your thighs.
Rest your forehead on the floor or a cushion.
Breathe slowly into your back for 30 to 60 seconds.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 holds, once a day or after exercise.
commonMistakes: Forcing the hips down when the knees are stiff.
warnings: Knee pain prevents full kneeling. Place a cushion between buttocks and heels.

faqs.q: Is child's pose safe in pregnancy?
faqs.a: With knees wide to make room for the bump, yes, for most women.

faqs.q: What if I can't reach my heels?
faqs.a: Put a pillow on your calves and rest on it.

exercises.title: Chin Tucks
exercises.summary: How to do chin tucks correctly. Steps, reps and common mistakes for neck pain and forward head posture, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Long hours looking down at screens let the head drift forward, which loads the joints and muscles at the back of the neck. Chin tucks switch on the deep neck flexors and gently lengthen the base of the skull. Done often, they help you notice and correct your posture during the day. You will often see it in our programmes for cervical spondylosis, cervical myelopathy and disc bulge, and it features in our neck pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit or stand tall with your shoulders relaxed and eyes looking straight ahead.
Slide your chin straight back, as if making a double chin. Keep your eyes level; don't nod down.
You should feel a gentle stretch at the base of the skull and light effort at the front of the neck.
Hold for 5 seconds, then relax without letting the head poke forward.
Progress by doing it lying on your back, pressing the back of the head gently into the pillow.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions with a 5 second hold, 2 to 3 times a day. Short, frequent sets during work breaks work better than one long session.
commonMistakes: Tipping the head down instead of sliding it back.
Pushing hard. It should be a gentle movement.
Shrugging the shoulders while tucking.
warnings: You get pain, tingling or numbness spreading into an arm.
You feel dizzy, get visual changes or a severe headache.

faqs.q: How long before chin tucks help?
faqs.a: Many people feel easier within a week or two. Posture habits take longer, so keep them going for several weeks.

faqs.q: Can I do chin tucks with a disc bulge?
faqs.a: Usually yes, and they are often part of treatment. If arm symptoms increase, stop and get assessed.

faqs.q: What are chin tucks?
faqs.a: Chin tucks are a small neck exercise where you glide your head straight back, as if making a double chin, to wake up the deep neck muscles that hold your head over your shoulders.

faqs.q: How are chin tucks performed?
faqs.a: Sit or stand tall with your shoulders relaxed. Look straight ahead. Keeping your eyes level, glide your head straight backwards. Your chin moves back, not down. Hold for 5 seconds. You should feel a gentle stretch at the base of the skull and light effort at the front of the neck. Relax back to the start and repeat. Start with 10 repetitions, two or three times a day.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of chin tucks?
faqs.a: They reduce neck ache from screen use, improve forward head posture, ease tension headaches from the base of the skull and are safe for most neck conditions. They are often part of rehab for cervical spondylosis, cervical myelopathy and concussion.

faqs.q: Which muscles do chin tucks target?
faqs.a: The deep neck flexors (longus colli and longus capitis), with a gentle stretch of the muscles at the base of the skull.

exercises.title: Clamshell Exercise
exercises.summary: Clamshell exercise for hip strength and knee pain. How to do it correctly, band progressions and common mistakes from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Clamshells strengthen the muscles that rotate the hip outwards and control the knee from collapsing inwards. You will often see it in our programmes for trochanteric bursitis, hip osteoarthritis and total hip replacement, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your side with hips and knees bent to about 45 degrees and feet together.
Keep your top hip stacked directly over the bottom hip.
Keeping the feet touching, lift the top knee as far as you can without the pelvis rolling back.
Hold 2 seconds, then lower slowly.
Add a resistance band just above the knees to progress.
exercises.howMuch: 12 to 15 repetitions each side, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Rolling the pelvis backwards to lift the knee higher.
Rushing.
warnings: Lying on the bottom hip is painful.

faqs.q: How high should the knee go?
faqs.a: Only as high as you can without the pelvis moving. That may be quite small.

faqs.q: Clamshells or side leg raises?
faqs.a: Both work the gluteus medius in different positions. We often use both.

exercises.title: Coordination Exercises
exercises.summary: Coordination exercises for adults and children. Examples for ataxia, stroke and developmental delay from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Coordination relies on the brain, especially the cerebellum, integrating sensory information to time movements. Practice improves accuracy and speed. It is a regular part of rehab plans for multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy and stroke, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Finger to nose: touch your nose, then a target held in front, alternating.
Heel to shin: lying down, slide one heel along the opposite shin.
Alternating taps: tap hands or feet alternately, speeding up gradually.
Ball skills: rolling, throwing and catching, bouncing.
For children: obstacle courses, hopscotch and clapping games.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 minutes a day, varied to keep it interesting.
warnings: Coordination worsens noticeably over weeks. This needs medical review.

faqs.q: Can coordination improve in adults?
faqs.a: Yes, with practice, depending on the cause.

faqs.q: How do you keep children engaged?
faqs.a: We build exercises into play.

exercises.title: Core Bracing
exercises.summary: Core and abdominal bracing technique for back pain. How to brace correctly while breathing, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: A light brace stiffens the trunk so forces pass through it more evenly. It gives confidence when returning to lifting after back pain. It is a regular part of rehab plans for lumbar spondylosis, disc bulge and spondylolisthesis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent, or stand tall.
Place your fingers just inside your hip bones.
Tighten your tummy muscles lightly all around, as if about to be poked in the stomach. You should feel firmness under the fingers.
Keep breathing normally throughout. Don't suck the tummy in.
Hold 10 seconds, then relax. Practise the brace during daily tasks such as lifting shopping.
exercises.howMuch: 10 holds of 10 seconds, twice a day, then apply it during other exercises.
commonMistakes: Holding the breath.
Bracing at maximum effort. Around a quarter of your maximum is enough for daily tasks.
warnings: Bracing increases pain or you feel pelvic floor heaviness.

faqs.q: Should I brace all day?
faqs.a: No. Use it for lifting and demanding tasks. Constant bracing is tiring and unnecessary.

faqs.q: Is bracing the same as drawing in?
faqs.a: No. Drawing in pulls the tummy button inwards. Bracing tightens the muscles without changing shape.

exercises.title: Core Strengthening
exercises.summary: Core strengthening exercises for back pain and sport. Planks, side planks, bridges and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The core includes the abdominals, back extensors, glutes, diaphragm and pelvic floor. Training them together improves trunk control during movement. Our physiotherapists use it most often for lumbar spondylosis, disc bulge and spondylolisthesis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Start with core bracing and dead bugs.
Front plank: forearms and toes (or knees) on the floor, body straight, hold 10 to 30 seconds.
Side plank: on one forearm and the side of the knees or feet, hold 10 to 30 seconds.
Combine with bird dogs and glute bridges.
Progress hold times before difficulty.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 5 exercises, 2 to 3 sets, 3 to 4 days a week.
commonMistakes: Holding the breath.
Sagging or piking the hips in a plank.
warnings: You're postnatal with abdominal separation or pelvic floor symptoms. Start with basic activation first.

faqs.q: Are sit-ups good for the core?
faqs.a: They have a place for some people, but planks and bracing exercises usually suit back pain better.

faqs.q: How long should I hold a plank?
faqs.a: Quality matters more than time. Stop when form breaks.

exercises.title: Crawling Exercises
exercises.summary: Crawling exercises for babies and children. Four-point play and obstacle ideas from Physiosolution pediatric physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Crawling builds shoulder stability, hip strength and alternating movement patterns. Our physiotherapists use it most often for down syndrome, dyslexia and autism, and it features in our pediatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Hands and knees rocking: support the baby in four-point position and rock gently.
Place toys just ahead to encourage reaching and moving.
Crawl over cushions and through tunnels for older children.
Animal walks: bear crawls and crab walks for school-age children.
exercises.howMuch: Daily play sessions.
warnings: Your child crawls using only one side, or drags a leg.

faqs.q: Is it okay if my baby bottom-shuffles?
faqs.a: Some babies skip crawling. Discuss if there are other concerns.

faqs.q: Why crawling for older children?
faqs.a: It builds strength and coordination in a fun way.

exercises.title: Dead Bug
exercises.summary: Dead bug exercise for core strength and back pain. Beginner to advanced versions with reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The challenge is keeping the pelvis and back still while the limbs move. That builds anti-extension control, which protects the back during lifting and sport. You will often see it in our programmes for lumbar spondylosis, disc bulge and spondylolisthesis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent at 90 degrees over your hips and arms pointing at the ceiling.
Gently press your lower back towards the floor and breathe out.
Slowly lower one heel to tap the floor, keeping the knee bent. Return.
Progress to lowering the opposite arm overhead at the same time.
Harder: straighten the leg as it lowers.
exercises.howMuch: 6 to 10 slow repetitions each side, 2 to 3 sets.
commonMistakes: Lower back arching off the floor as the leg lowers.
Rushing.
warnings: You notice doming along the middle of the tummy after pregnancy. Start with easier core work first.

faqs.q: What is doming?
faqs.a: A ridge along the midline of the abdomen, often seen with abdominal separation after pregnancy.

faqs.q: How do I make it easier?
faqs.a: Keep both feet on the floor and move one arm at a time.

exercises.title: Deep Breathing and Thoracic Expansion
exercises.summary: Deep breathing and thoracic expansion exercises after surgery and for chest conditions. Technique from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: After surgery or with reduced mobility, lung bases don't fully inflate. Deep breaths with a hold improve air entry and help clear mucus. It is a regular part of rehab plans for asthma, spinal cord injury and ankylosing spondylitis, and it features in our post-surgical rehabilitation programmes.
steps: Sit upright or lie propped up.
Place hands on your lower ribs.
Breathe in slowly and deeply, feeling the ribs expand into your hands.
Hold for 3 seconds.
Breathe out gently. Do 3 to 4 breaths, then rest with normal breathing.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 4 deep breaths, repeated every hour while awake after surgery.
warnings: You have increasing breathlessness, fever or coloured sputum.

faqs.q: Why the pause between sets?
faqs.a: Too many deep breaths in a row can cause dizziness.

faqs.q: How does this help mucus?
faqs.a: Air gets behind secretions, making coughing more effective.

exercises.title: Diaphragmatic Breathing
exercises.summary: Diaphragmatic (belly) breathing and breathing control. How to do it for asthma, anxiety, postnatal recovery and pelvic health, from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Shallow upper-chest breathing wastes effort and increases tension. Using the diaphragm improves efficiency and calms the nervous system. You will often see it in our programmes for asthma, urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse, and it features in our pregnancy and postnatal physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent, or sit supported.
Place one hand on your chest and one on your belly.
Breathe in gently through your nose, letting the belly rise while the chest stays still.
Breathe out slowly through the mouth, letting the belly fall.
Keep it relaxed; don't force big breaths.
exercises.howMuch: 5 to 10 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day, and whenever you feel breathless.
warnings: You feel dizzy or tingly. Slow down and breathe less deeply.

faqs.q: How does this help the pelvic floor?
faqs.a: The diaphragm and pelvic floor move together. Breathing well supports pelvic floor rehab.

faqs.q: Can it help anxiety?
faqs.a: Slow breathing often reduces feelings of stress.

exercises.title: Dumbbell Exercises
exercises.summary: Dumbbell exercises for rehab, osteoporosis and strength. Key exercises, safe technique and how to progress, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Progressive resistance training builds muscle and bone strength. Weights make progress easy to track. You will often see it in our programmes for osteoporosis, rotator cuff injury and knee osteoarthritis, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Start with a weight you can lift 10 to 12 times with good form.
Core exercises: goblet squat, Romanian deadlift, bent-over row, overhead press, biceps curl and calf raises.
Lift in 2 seconds, lower in 3 seconds.
Keep the back neutral and core braced.
Increase weight by small amounts when 12 repetitions are easy.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, 2 to 3 days a week.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back when lifting from the floor.
Adding weight too quickly.
warnings: You have osteoporosis; avoid loaded spinal bending and twisting.

faqs.q: Are weights safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Yes, with appropriate supervision and progression. Strength training benefits people of all ages.

faqs.q: How heavy should I lift?
faqs.a: Heavy enough that the last couple of repetitions feel challenging but still controlled.

exercises.title: Elbow Flexion and Extension
exercises.summary: Elbow flexion and extension exercises after fractures and stiffness. Range and strengthening versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Range exercises prevent a permanently stiff elbow. Strengthening restores lifting and pushing ability. It is a regular part of rehab plans for elbow fractures, forearm fractures and biceps tendonitis, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit with your elbow supported on a table or pillow.
Slowly bend the elbow as far as possible, using the other hand to assist.
Hold 5 seconds, then straighten as far as possible and hold.
Strengthening: hold a light weight and do biceps curls, then triceps extensions overhead or lying down.
exercises.howMuch: Range: 10 repetitions, 3 to 4 times a day. Strength: 10 to 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets.
commonMistakes: Forcing painful stretches; the elbow reacts badly to force.
Swinging the weight.
warnings: The elbow becomes hot and increasingly stiff despite exercise.

faqs.q: Why is the elbow so prone to stiffness?
faqs.a: Its joint capsule reacts strongly to injury and immobilisation.

faqs.q: Should I use heat before?
faqs.a: Heat can make the stretch more comfortable.

exercises.title: Elbow Isometric Exercises
exercises.summary: Elbow isometric exercises for tennis elbow, golfer's elbow and early rehab. Positions and holds from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Isometrics load tendons at a controllable level. Many people find they ease tendon pain for a while afterwards. You will often see it in our programmes for tennis elbow, Golfer's elbow and elbow fractures, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Wrist extension isometric: rest your forearm on a table, palm down. Place the other hand on the back of the hand and push up into it without moving.
Wrist flexion isometric: turn the palm up and push up against the other hand.
Elbow bend isometric: press the palm up against the underside of a table.
Hold each 30 to 45 seconds at a moderate effort.
exercises.howMuch: 5 holds, 1 to 2 times a day.
commonMistakes: Pushing so hard that pain increases.
warnings: Pain increases the next day or doesn't settle after two weeks.

faqs.q: How hard should I push?
faqs.a: Aim for a moderate effort with pain under about 3 out of 10.

faqs.q: When do I progress?
faqs.a: When holds are comfortable, we move to slow weighted movements.

exercises.title: Fall Prevention Exercises
exercises.summary: Fall prevention exercises for seniors. Strength and balance routine, safety tips and home setup from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Falls often result from weak legs, poor balance and slow reactions. Targeted exercise improves all three. You will often see it in our programmes for osteoporosis, Parkinson's disease and dementia, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit to stand: 10 repetitions.
Calf and toe raises holding a counter: 10 each.
Single leg stand: 10 to 30 seconds each leg, holding on.
Heel-to-toe standing and walking along the counter.
Side steps along the counter.
Make the home safer too: remove loose rugs, add night lights and grab rails.
exercises.howMuch: At least 3 times a week, 30 minutes a session, continued long term.
warnings: You've had a fall recently, feel dizzy or have blackouts. Get a medical review.

faqs.q: How long before falls reduce?
faqs.a: Benefits build over months of regular practice.

faqs.q: Do you assess fall risk?
faqs.a: Yes, including balance tests and a home review on home visits.

exercises.title: Fine Motor Exercises
exercises.summary: Fine motor exercises for hand dexterity after stroke, in Parkinson's and for children. Practical activities from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Dexterity depends on strength, sensation and precise control. Graded tasks retrain each. It is a regular part of rehab plans for stroke, Parkinson's disease and cerebral palsy, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Pick up coins, beads or beans and place them in a container.
Button and unbutton a shirt on a table.
Roll, pinch and pull therapy putty.
Stack small blocks or turn cards over.
Trace shapes and letters with a pen.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 minutes, 1 to 2 times a day.
warnings: Hand pain or cramping persists.

faqs.q: Does handwriting improve in Parkinson's?
faqs.a: Specific training with large, deliberate movements can help.

faqs.q: What toys help children?
faqs.a: Pegboards, stacking cups and play dough are good starting points.

exercises.title: Finger Flexion and Extension
exercises.summary: Finger flexion and extension exercises for hand stiffness after injury or surgery. Technique and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Finger joints stiffen within days if they don't move. Regular full-range movement keeps tendons gliding and joints mobile. It is a regular part of rehab plans for hand fractures, wrist fracture and trigger finger, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Rest your forearm on a table.
Make a full fist, bending all finger joints, and hold 3 seconds.
Open the hand fully, straightening all fingers, and hold 3 seconds.
Block each joint separately: hold the finger below a joint and bend only that joint.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions, every 2 to 3 hours while stiffness is present.
commonMistakes: Not reaching full bend or straighten.
Skipping the blocking exercises.
warnings: A finger won't straighten on its own, as in mallet finger. It may need a splint rather than exercise.

faqs.q: Should I exercise a finger in a splint?
faqs.a: Only the joints your therapist allows. Some must be kept still.

faqs.q: Why is my hand so swollen?
faqs.a: Swelling is common after injury. Keeping the hand raised and moving the fingers helps.

exercises.title: Functional Movement Training
exercises.summary: Functional movement training for stroke, neurological and elderly rehab. Task-based practice explained by Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Task-specific practice produces better gains in those tasks than general exercise alone. It is a regular part of rehab plans for stroke, Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Identify priority tasks with the person and family.
Break each into steps, e.g. rolling, pushing up, swinging legs off the bed.
Practise each step, then the whole task.
Adjust the environment: bed height, rails, furniture layout.
Repeat daily in the real setting.
exercises.howMuch: Daily, built into routine care.
warnings: A task causes pain or falls.

faqs.q: Is this done at home?
faqs.a: Home is the best place because the practice happens where the task is needed.

faqs.q: How does it differ from exercise?
faqs.a: It trains the movement itself in context, not just the muscles.

exercises.title: Functional Reach Exercises
exercises.summary: Functional reach exercises for balance and fall prevention. Forward and sideways reaching from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Reaching shifts the centre of mass towards the edge of the base of support. Practising increases the distance you can safely reach. Our physiotherapists use it most often for stroke, Parkinson's disease and spinal cord injury, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand side-on to a counter, holding it with one hand.
Reach forward with the other arm as far as you can without stepping.
Hold 3 seconds and return.
Reach sideways, across the body and down towards the floor.
Seated version: sit on a firm chair and reach in all directions.
exercises.howMuch: 10 reaches in each direction, once a day.
warnings: You feel unsafe; practise seated first.

faqs.q: What's the functional reach test?
faqs.a: A measure of how far you can reach forward; shorter distances indicate higher fall risk.

faqs.q: Can I do this seated after spinal cord injury?
faqs.a: Yes, seated reaching trains trunk balance.

exercises.title: Functional Strengthening
exercises.summary: Functional strengthening and functional rehabilitation exercises. Lifting, carrying and reaching patterns from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Strength gained lying on a mat doesn't always transfer to daily tasks. Practising real movements with load bridges that gap. You will often see it in our programmes for osteoporosis, lumbar spondylosis and total knee replacement, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Squat to lift: lift a light box from a chair using a squat, keeping the back neutral.
Farmer's carry: walk holding a bag in each hand, standing tall.
Step and reach: step forward and reach to a shelf.
Floor transfer: practise getting down to and up from the floor safely.
Progress load and complexity gradually.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 5 movements, 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10, 2 to 3 days a week.
commonMistakes: Adding load before technique is steady.
warnings: A specific task consistently triggers pain.

faqs.q: What does functional mean?
faqs.a: Relevant to what you actually need to do: your work, home tasks or sport.

faqs.q: Is this for athletes only?
faqs.a: No. It's just as important for older adults and after surgery.

exercises.title: Gait Training
exercises.summary: Gait training for walking recovery after stroke, surgery and Parkinson's. What it involves and how progress is made, from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Walking patterns change after injury or illness. Gait training identifies the problems and practises better movement, repeated enough to become automatic. It is a regular part of rehab plans for stroke, Parkinson's disease and cerebral palsy, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Assessment: we look at step length, heel strike, knee control, trunk posture and speed.
Drills: marching, step-throughs, heel-toe practice and weight shifting.
Walking with cues: counting, a metronome beat or floor markers, especially in Parkinson's.
Walking aid training: using a stick, crutches or walker correctly, and progressing off them.
Real-world practice: turns, uneven ground, slopes and doorways.
exercises.howMuch: Daily walking practice, with specific drills 3 to 5 times a week as prescribed.
warnings: Falls or near-falls increase.

faqs.q: Why does Parkinson's respond to rhythm cues?
faqs.a: External cues can bypass some of the brain pathways affected by the condition.

faqs.q: When can I stop using my walker?
faqs.a: When balance and strength tests show it's safe. We test this rather than guess.

exercises.title: Glute Bridge
exercises.summary: Glute bridge exercise for back, hip and knee pain. How to do it properly, sets, reps and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Strong glutes stabilise the pelvis, take load off the lower back and control the knee. The bridge builds that strength in a position most people can manage. Our physiotherapists use it most often for lumbar spondylosis, disc bulge and hip osteoarthritis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat and hip width apart.
Tighten your tummy gently and squeeze your buttocks.
Lift your hips until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
Hold 3 to 5 seconds, then lower slowly.
Progress with a band around the knees, a longer hold, or a single-leg bridge.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back at the top instead of using the glutes.
Pushing through the toes.
Feeling it mostly in the hamstrings. Bring the feet a little closer.
warnings: Lower back pain increases rather than easing over a week.

faqs.q: Why do my hamstrings cramp?
faqs.a: Feet too far away or glutes not switching on. Move the feet closer and squeeze the buttocks first.

faqs.q: Can I bridge after hip replacement?
faqs.a: Usually yes, early in rehab. Follow your surgeon's precautions.

faqs.q: What is the glute bridge?
faqs.a: The glute bridge lifts the hips from lying on your back with knees bent.

exercises.title: Grip Strengthening
exercises.summary: Grip strengthening exercises with a ball or putty. Progressions for hand, wrist and elbow rehab from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Grip uses forearm and hand muscles together. Regaining strength helps with carrying, opening jars and holding tools. Our physiotherapists use it most often for wrist fracture, hand fractures and tennis elbow, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Hold a soft ball or putty in your palm.
Squeeze firmly with all fingers, hold 3 to 5 seconds, then relax fully.
Progress to firmer putty or longer holds.
Add pinch grip: squeeze the putty between thumb and each fingertip.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 squeezes, 2 to 3 sets, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Squeezing through pain, especially with tennis elbow.
Holding the breath.
warnings: Grip is painful at the outer elbow. Start with the elbow straight and a lighter effort.

faqs.q: What if grip hurts my elbow?
faqs.a: That's common in tennis elbow. We adjust the position and load.

faqs.q: Is a hand grip exerciser better than a ball?
faqs.a: Both work. Adjustable trainers make progression easier.

exercises.title: Hamstring Curls
exercises.summary: Hamstring curl exercise for knee strength and ACL rehab. Standing, prone and band versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Strong hamstrings resist forward movement of the shin bone and support the knee during sport and daily movement. It is a regular part of rehab plans for ACL tear, PCL injury and meniscal injury, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Standing: hold a chair back. Bend one knee to bring the heel towards your buttock, keeping the thighs level.
Lying face down: bend the knee to bring the heel up, then lower slowly.
Band: lie face down with a band around the ankle anchored low in front, and curl against it.
Lower slowly each time.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions each leg, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Moving the thigh forward instead of bending the knee.
Arching the back when lying.
warnings: After ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft, follow your surgeon's timeline for resisted curls.

faqs.q: Why wait after a hamstring graft?
faqs.a: The donor site needs time to heal before it is loaded.

faqs.q: My hamstring cramps. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Common early on. Reduce effort and range, and build up gradually.

exercises.title: Hamstring Stretch
exercises.summary: Hamstring stretch for tight hamstrings, knee and back pain. Lying, seated and standing versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Regular stretching improves hamstring length, which makes forward bending, straightening the knee and running more comfortable. Our physiotherapists use it most often for knee osteoarthritis, total knee replacement and hamstring strain, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lying (safest for the back): lie on your back and loop a towel around one foot.
Straighten the knee and raise the leg until you feel a stretch behind the thigh.
Hold 30 seconds, keeping the other leg relaxed.
Seated: sit on the edge of a chair, one leg straight with heel on the floor. Lean forward from the hips with a straight back.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds of 30 seconds each leg, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back to reach further.
Bouncing.
warnings: Stretching causes tingling or pain down the back of the leg. This may be nerve tension, not muscle.

faqs.q: How do I tell nerve tension from tight hamstrings?
faqs.a: Nerve symptoms are often burning or tingling and change when you move your neck or ankle. We test this.

faqs.q: Should I stretch before sport?
faqs.a: Dynamic warm-ups are better before sport. Save longer holds for afterwards.

exercises.title: Head Control Exercises
exercises.summary: Head control exercises for babies and children with developmental delay. Activities and milestones from Physiosolution pediatric physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Neck and trunk strength develop through play in different positions. Children with low tone or neurological conditions may need extra practice. You will often see it in our programmes for down syndrome, torticollis and cerebral palsy, and it features in our pediatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Tummy time with toys at eye level.
Supported sitting on your lap, facing you, while you talk and sing.
Pull to sit: holding the baby's forearms, gently bring them from lying to sitting, watching that the head follows.
Side-lying play to encourage turning.
exercises.howMuch: Several short sessions daily, as part of play.
warnings: Head lag persists beyond around 4 months, or head control seems to be lost.

faqs.q: When should a baby hold their head steady?
faqs.a: Most babies have good head control by around 4 months.

faqs.q: My baby prefers turning one way. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Persistent preference needs checking for torticollis.

exercises.title: Heel Slides
exercises.summary: Heel slides exercise to improve knee bending after surgery. Technique, reps and range targets from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Repeated bending prevents scar tissue from limiting knee movement. Enough bend is needed for climbing stairs and getting up from a chair. You will often see it in our programmes for total knee replacement, ACL tear and patellar fracture, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back with legs straight. A plastic bag under the heel reduces friction.
Slowly slide your heel towards your buttock, bending the knee as far as you can.
Hold 5 seconds at the end, then slide back.
For more bend, loop a towel around the foot and pull gently.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions, 3 times a day in early rehab.
commonMistakes: Lifting the hip or twisting the leg.
Stopping short of the stretch point.
warnings: Bending is not improving week to week after knee replacement. Early action matters.

faqs.q: How much knee bend do I need?
faqs.a: Around 110 degrees for most daily activities, more for squatting or sitting on the floor.

faqs.q: Should heel slides hurt?
faqs.a: A stretching discomfort is expected after surgery. Sharp pain is not.

exercises.title: Heel Walking
exercises.summary: Heel walking exercise for shin strength and ankle control. How to do it safely and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Walking on the heels works the dorsiflexors in a dynamic, weight-bearing way, and challenges balance. You will often see it in our programmes for ankle sprain, flat foot and foot drop, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand next to a wall or counter.
Lift your toes and the front of your feet off the ground.
Take small steps forward on your heels.
Keep an upright posture; don't lean back or stick your bottom out.
Walk 10 metres, rest and repeat.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 4 lengths of 10 metres, once a day.
commonMistakes: Bending at the hips.
Taking large steps.
warnings: It causes pain at the front of the shin, which may suggest shin splints.

faqs.q: Does heel walking help foot drop?
faqs.a: If some movement exists, it can help build strength. We decide based on assessment.

faqs.q: Can I do it barefoot?
faqs.a: Yes, on a safe, non-slip surface.

exercises.title: Hip Abduction
exercises.summary: Hip abduction exercise for glute medius strength, hip and knee pain. Side-lying, standing and band versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Every step involves a moment standing on one leg. The gluteus medius stops the opposite hip dropping. Strengthening it improves walking and reduces strain on the hip and knee. You will often see it in our programmes for trochanteric bursitis, hip osteoarthritis and total hip replacement, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Side-lying: lie on your side with the bottom knee bent and the top leg straight in line with your body.
Turn the top toes slightly down and lift the leg towards the ceiling, leading with the heel.
Lift about 30 to 40 centimetres, hold 2 seconds and lower slowly.
Standing: hold a support and lift the leg out to the side without leaning.
Progress with an ankle weight or band around the ankles.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions each side, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Rolling the pelvis backwards so the hip flexors do the work.
Lifting too high.
warnings: Side-lying is painful on the bottom hip; use the standing version or a cushion.

faqs.q: I feel it at the front of the hip. Why?
faqs.a: The leg is probably drifting forward. Keep it slightly behind your body line.

faqs.q: Does this help trochanteric bursitis?
faqs.a: Strengthening the gluteal tendons is a main part of treatment. We adjust the exercise to avoid compressing the sore area.

exercises.title: Hip Adduction
exercises.summary: Hip adduction exercises for groin strength and knee support. Ball squeeze and side-lying versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The adductors work with the glutes to keep the pelvis balanced. Ball squeezes are a simple way to switch them on, and they often co-activate the pelvic floor. You will often see it in our programmes for hip osteoarthritis, genu varum (bow legs) and knee osteoarthritis, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Ball squeeze: lie on your back with knees bent and a small ball or folded pillow between your knees.
Squeeze the ball for 5 to 10 seconds, then relax.
Side-lying: lie on your side, top leg bent with the foot in front of the bottom knee.
Lift the straight bottom leg a few centimetres, hold 2 seconds and lower.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Squeezing so hard the groin hurts.
Holding your breath.
warnings: You feel sharp groin pain, especially after sport.

faqs.q: Do adductors matter for footballers?
faqs.a: Yes. Adductor strength is linked with fewer groin injuries.

faqs.q: Can I do this after hip replacement?
faqs.a: Some approaches restrict crossing the midline. Check your precautions first.

exercises.title: Hip Extension
exercises.summary: Hip extension exercise for glute strength after hip pain or surgery. Standing and prone versions with reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The glutes drive the leg back when walking. Weakness shows as a shortened stride and difficulty climbing stairs. You will often see it in our programmes for total hip replacement, hip fracture and hip osteoarthritis, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Standing: hold a chair back or counter for support.
Keeping your trunk upright and knee straight, move one leg backwards a short distance.
Squeeze the buttock at the end, hold 2 seconds, then return.
Lying: lie face down, tighten the buttock and lift a straight leg a few centimetres off the bed.
Progress with an ankle weight or band.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions each leg, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Leaning forward to lift the leg higher.
Arching the lower back.
warnings: After hip replacement, check which movements are allowed in your surgeon's precautions.

faqs.q: How far back should the leg go?
faqs.a: Only a short distance. Movement beyond that comes from the lower back.

faqs.q: Can I do this after a hip fracture?
faqs.a: Usually, as part of rehab, when weight-bearing status allows.

exercises.title: Hip Flexion
exercises.summary: Hip flexion exercises for walking, stairs and hip rehab. Seated marching, standing knee lifts and progressions from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: The hip flexors lift the leg forward. Training them improves step height and reduces the risk of tripping. Our physiotherapists use it most often for total hip replacement, hip fracture and stroke, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Seated: sit upright in a firm chair. Lift one knee a few centimetres off the seat, hold 2 seconds, lower.
Standing: hold a support and lift one knee towards hip height, like marching.
Lying: slide your heel up the bed bending the hip and knee, then slide back down.
Progress with an ankle weight.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions each leg, 2 sets, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Leaning back in the chair to lift the leg.
Lifting past 90 degrees if you have hip replacement precautions.
warnings: Pain at the front of the hip increases, which may indicate tendon irritation.

faqs.q: Are there limits after hip replacement?
faqs.a: Some surgical approaches limit bending the hip past 90 degrees for several weeks. Follow your surgeon's advice.

faqs.q: Why is lifting the leg hard after a stroke?
faqs.a: Weakness and altered control on the affected side. Repetition and specific training help.

exercises.title: Hip Flexor Stretch
exercises.summary: Hip flexor stretch for tight hips and lower back pain. Half-kneeling technique, hold time and mistakes from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stretching the iliopsoas and rectus femoris restores hip extension, which is needed for a normal walking stride and upright standing. Our physiotherapists use it most often for hip impingement, hip osteoarthritis and lumbar spondylosis, and it features in our lower back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Kneel on your right knee on a cushion, left foot flat in front with the knee at 90 degrees.
Tuck your tailbone under and gently squeeze the right buttock.
Shift your weight slightly forward until you feel a stretch at the front of the right hip.
Keep your trunk upright; don't lean back.
Hold 30 seconds and switch sides.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 holds per side, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back instead of tucking the pelvis.
Lunging too far forward.
warnings: You feel pinching deep in the front of the hip. Hip impingement may need a modified position.

faqs.q: I can't kneel. What else can I do?
faqs.a: Lie on the edge of a bed and let one leg hang off while hugging the other knee.

faqs.q: Why does my back feel better after?
faqs.a: Tight hip flexors pull on the lower spine. Easing them reduces that pull.

exercises.title: Hip Rotation Exercises
exercises.summary: Hip rotation exercises for stiffness and hip arthritis. Seated rotation, figure-four and band exercises from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Rotation exercises keep the hip capsule mobile and strengthen the muscles that control rotation during walking and turning. Our physiotherapists use it most often for hip osteoarthritis, hip impingement and hip labral tear, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Seated rotation: sit upright on a high chair with knees at 90 degrees. Keeping the knee still, swing the foot outwards (internal rotation), then inwards (external rotation).
Lying: lie on your back with knees bent and let one knee fall outwards gently, then bring it back.
Band: sit with a band around the ankle anchored to the side and rotate the foot against it.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions each direction, 2 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Moving the knee instead of turning the thigh.
Forcing painful end range.
warnings: You have hip replacement precautions restricting rotation.
Rotation causes sharp groin pain or clicking.

faqs.q: Why is internal rotation limited in arthritis?
faqs.a: It's often the first movement affected as the joint capsule stiffens.

faqs.q: Is clicking a problem?
faqs.a: Painless clicking is common. Painful catching may need assessment.

exercises.title: Incentive Spirometry
exercises.summary: Incentive spirometry exercises after surgery. How to use the device correctly, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Visual feedback motivates slow, deep breaths that open the small air sacs of the lungs. You will often see it in our programmes for spinal fusion, total hip replacement and spinal cord injury, and it features in our post-surgical rehabilitation programmes.
steps: Sit upright.
Breathe out normally, then seal your lips around the mouthpiece.
Breathe in slowly and deeply, raising the indicator towards your target.
Hold your breath for 3 to 5 seconds.
Breathe out and rest. Cough to clear any mucus.
exercises.howMuch: 10 breaths every hour while awake after surgery, or as your team advises.
warnings: You feel dizzy. Rest between breaths.

faqs.q: What target should I aim for?
faqs.a: Your hospital team usually sets one based on your size and surgery.

faqs.q: Why breathe in slowly?
faqs.a: Slow breaths fill the lungs more evenly than fast gasps.

exercises.title: Isometric Exercises
exercises.summary: Isometric exercises explained. How they work, when to use them and examples for knee, shoulder, neck and back, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Isometrics strengthen muscles at the angle they are held. They can reduce pain in tendinopathy and maintain strength when movement is limited. You will often see it in our programmes for rheumatoid arthritis, tendinitis and knee osteoarthritis, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Choose a position that is comfortable, such as a quadriceps set, wall squat or wall press.
Contract the muscle to a moderate effort without moving the joint.
Hold 5 to 45 seconds depending on the goal.
Breathe normally throughout.
Relax fully between holds.
exercises.howMuch: 5 to 10 holds per exercise, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Holding the breath, which raises blood pressure.
Using maximal effort too early.
warnings: You have uncontrolled high blood pressure. Keep effort moderate and breathe.

faqs.q: Are isometrics effective for strength?
faqs.a: Yes, especially early on. Movement-based training is added later for full-range strength.

faqs.q: Do isometrics raise blood pressure?
faqs.a: Briefly, especially with breath holding. Breathe steadily.

exercises.title: IT Band Stretch
exercises.summary: IT band stretch for outer knee and hip pain. Standing cross-over and lying versions, and what really helps, from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stretching the tensor fascia lata and gluteal muscles, which pull on the IT band, may reduce outer thigh tightness. Our physiotherapists use it most often for trochanteric bursitis, knee osteoarthritis and genu varum (bow legs), and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand next to a wall with your right side towards it.
Cross your left leg in front of your right.
Push your right hip towards the wall until you feel a stretch on the outer right hip.
Hold 30 seconds, switch sides.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds each side, once a day.
commonMistakes: Bending forward.
warnings: Outer knee pain during running persists. Load management and hip strength usually matter more.

faqs.q: Does foam rolling the IT band help?
faqs.a: It may reduce sensitivity briefly. It does not lengthen the band.

faqs.q: What causes IT band pain in runners?
faqs.a: Usually training load and hip control. Strength work is key.

exercises.title: Joint Replacement Rehabilitation Exercises
exercises.summary: Rehabilitation exercises after joint replacement: knee, hip and shoulder. Principles, stages and expectations from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The surgery replaces the worn surfaces; rehabilitation makes the joint work well. Our physiotherapists use it most often for total knee replacement, total hip replacement and shoulder arthropathy, and it features in our post-surgical rehabilitation programmes.
steps: Early circulation and breathing exercises.
Range of motion within your surgeon's limits.
Muscle activation and progressive strengthening.
Walking or arm function training.
Return to daily activities and hobbies.
exercises.howMuch: Several short sessions a day early on, then daily programmes over months.
warnings: Increasing pain, redness, fever, wound discharge or calf swelling.

faqs.q: How long is recovery?
faqs.a: Most people see major improvement by 3 months, with gains continuing up to a year.

faqs.q: Can rehab be done at home?
faqs.a: Yes. Many patients do early rehab at home with our visiting physiotherapists.

exercises.title: Kegel Exercises
exercises.summary: Kegel exercises (pelvic floor exercises) for incontinence, prolapse and after childbirth. Correct technique and routine from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: A strong, well coordinated pelvic floor closes the bladder outlet when you cough, sneeze or lift, and supports the pelvic organs. Our physiotherapists use it most often for urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse, and it features in our women's health physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit, lie or stand comfortably and breathe normally.
Squeeze and lift the muscles as if stopping wind and holding in urine at the same time.
Hold for up to 10 seconds, then relax fully for the same time.
Then do 10 quick squeezes, relaxing between each.
Practise "the knack": squeeze before you cough, sneeze or lift.
exercises.howMuch: Up to 10 long holds and 10 quick squeezes, 3 times a day, for at least 3 months.
commonMistakes: Squeezing the buttocks, thighs or tummy instead.
Holding the breath.
Stopping urine flow regularly as practice.
warnings: You feel pain or can't feel the muscles working. An internal assessment by a pelvic health physiotherapist may help.

faqs.q: How long until I see results?
faqs.a: Often 6 to 12 weeks of regular practice.

faqs.q: Are Kegels always right?
faqs.a: Not for everyone. Some people have overactive pelvic floors and need relaxation instead.

exercises.title: Knee Extension Stretch
exercises.summary: Knee extension stretch (heel prop) to straighten the knee after surgery. How long to hold and tips from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
