steps: Stand next to a wall or door frame with the elbow bent at 90 degrees and tucked at your side.
External rotation: press the back of the wrist outwards into the door frame.
Internal rotation: press the palm inwards into the frame.
Flexion: face the wall and press your fist forward into it.
Abduction: stand side-on and press the outside of the elbow into the wall.
Hold each for 10 to 30 seconds at a comfortable effort.
exercises.howMuch: 5 holds in each direction, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Pushing hard enough to cause pain.
Letting the shoulder shrug.
warnings: Pain increases the next day in a way that doesn't settle.

faqs.q: How long should I hold?
faqs.a: Start at 10 seconds. For tendon pain, longer holds of 30 to 45 seconds may be used under guidance.

faqs.q: When do I move on to band exercises?
faqs.a: When the holds are pain-free at moderate effort.

faqs.q: What are shoulder isometric exercises?
faqs.a: Shoulder isometric exercises press the arm into a wall or your hand without moving the joint.

faqs.q: How are shoulder isometric exercises performed?
faqs.a: Forward: fist into the wall in front. Backward: elbow into the wall behind. Outward: back of the wrist into the door frame beside you. Inward: palm into the door frame. Out to the side: side of the elbow into the wall.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of shoulder isometric exercises?
faqs.a: They build strength when movement is painful or restricted, making them ideal early after injury or surgery. They are often part of rehab for rotator cuff injury, supraspinatus tendinitis and shoulder impingement.

faqs.q: Which muscles do shoulder isometric exercises target?
faqs.a: The rotator cuff and deltoid, depending on direction.

exercises.title: Shoulder Stretch
exercises.summary: Cross-body shoulder stretch for shoulder tightness. Technique and hold times from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stretching the posterior shoulder improves internal rotation and cross-body reach. You will often see it in our programmes for shoulder impingement and rotator cuff injury, and it features in our frozen shoulder physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand or sit tall.
Bring one arm across your chest at shoulder height.
Use the other hand to gently pull the arm closer, holding above the elbow.
Keep the shoulder down, away from the ear.
Hold 30 seconds, switch sides.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds each side, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Rotating the trunk.
Pulling on the elbow joint itself.
warnings: The stretch causes pinching at the front of the shoulder.

faqs.q: Is this good for frozen shoulder?
faqs.a: It can help once the painful phase settles.

faqs.q: Why do throwers stretch this?
faqs.a: Throwing tightens the back of the shoulder over time.

exercises.title: Sideways Walking
exercises.summary: Sideways walking (side stepping) exercise for balance and hip strength. Progressions including band side steps from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Side stepping works the hip abductors and trains weight shifting from side to side. It is a regular part of rehab plans for hip osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and stroke, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand facing a counter with hands resting on it.
Step to the side with one foot, then bring the other to meet it.
Keep toes pointing forward and trunk upright.
Go 10 steps one way, then back.
Progress by adding a band around the knees or ankles.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 4 lengths, once a day.
warnings: You feel unsteady even with support.

faqs.q: Why sideways?
faqs.a: Falls sideways often lead to hip fractures. Training this direction improves protective reactions.

faqs.q: Can I do it with a walker?
faqs.a: Some people can, with guidance.

exercises.title: Single Leg Balance
exercises.summary: Single leg balance exercise for ankle sprains and fall prevention. Progressions from eyes open to unstable surfaces, from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Ankle ligaments contain sensors that tell the brain where the joint is. Injury disrupts these signals, and balance training restores them. It is a regular part of rehab plans for ankle sprain, ankle instability and ACL tear, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand next to a counter with fingertips resting on it.
Lift one foot off the floor and balance on the other.
Keep a soft knee and upright posture.
Progress: take hands off, then close your eyes, then stand on a cushion.
Advanced: throw and catch a ball while balancing.
exercises.howMuch: 30 seconds, 3 times each leg, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Locking the knee.
Progressing too quickly before steady at each stage.
warnings: You fall or feel very unsteady. Always practise near support.

faqs.q: How long should I be able to stand on one leg?
faqs.a: It varies with age. Under 10 seconds in older adults can signal higher fall risk.

faqs.q: Does it really prevent sprains?
faqs.a: Balance training is well supported for reducing repeat ankle sprains.

exercises.title: Single Leg Bridge
exercises.summary: Single leg bridge exercise for glute strength and pelvic control. Technique and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Working one side at a time reveals and corrects side-to-side differences in strength, which matter in running and jumping. Our physiotherapists use it most often for hamstring strain, hip labral tear and patellar tendonitis, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat.
Straighten one leg in line with the other thigh, or hug that knee to your chest for an easier version.
Push through the heel of the bent leg and lift the hips.
Keep the pelvis level; don't let one side drop.
Hold 3 seconds, lower slowly.
exercises.howMuch: 8 to 12 repetitions each leg, 2 to 3 sets, 3 to 4 days a week.
commonMistakes: Pelvis twisting or dropping on the lifted leg side.
Arching the back.
warnings: It brings on hamstring cramp or pain at the back of the knee repeatedly.

faqs.q: When can I progress from a normal bridge?
faqs.a: When you can do 3 sets of 15 double-leg bridges with good control.

faqs.q: How do I make it harder?
faqs.a: Place the foot on a step or add a pause at the top.

exercises.title: Sit to Stand
exercises.summary: Sit to stand exercise for leg strength, balance and independence. Technique, reps and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Rising from a chair uses the quadriceps and glutes, and requires shifting weight forward over the feet. Regular practice builds strength and independence, and the number you can do in 30 seconds is a standard measure of leg strength in older adults. It is a regular part of rehab plans for total hip replacement, hip fracture and stroke, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit towards the front of a firm chair with feet hip width apart and slightly behind the knees.
Lean your trunk forward over your feet ("nose over toes").
Push through both feet and stand up fully.
Sit back down slowly, reaching back with your bottom rather than dropping.
Use your hands on the armrests at first, then progress to arms crossed.
exercises.howMuch: 8 to 12 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once or twice a day. Use a higher chair if you can't manage from a standard one.
commonMistakes: Not leaning forward enough, so you fall back.
Letting the knees collapse inwards.
Dropping into the chair.
warnings: You feel dizzy on standing.
You're unsteady; have someone nearby or use a stable support.

faqs.q: How many should I be able to do?
faqs.a: It varies with age. We test it and set a target.

faqs.q: Is this safe after knee replacement?
faqs.a: Yes. It's a key goal in rehab. Start with a higher seat.

exercises.title: Sitting Balance Exercises
exercises.summary: Sitting balance exercises for babies and children with delays. Play-based activities from Physiosolution pediatric physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Trunk strength and protective reactions develop through supported sitting practice. Our physiotherapists use it most often for down syndrome, cerebral palsy and spina bifida, and it features in our pediatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit the child on the floor with support at the hips.
Offer toys in different directions to encourage reaching.
Gently tip them slightly to encourage saving reactions with the hands.
Progress to sitting on a small bench or therapy ball with support.
exercises.howMuch: Short, frequent play sessions.
warnings: Sitting unsupported hasn't developed by around 9 months.

faqs.q: When do babies sit alone?
faqs.a: Usually between 6 and 9 months.

faqs.q: Should I use baby seats?
faqs.a: Occasionally is fine. Floor play builds more strength.

exercises.title: Spinal Cord Injury Exercises
exercises.summary: Spinal cord injury exercises: strength, range of motion, breathing and transfers. Guidance from Physiosolution neuro physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Exercise maintains function, reduces complications and supports independence. It is a regular part of rehab plans for spinal cord injury, quadriplegia and cauda equina syndrome, and it features in our paralysis physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Range of motion and stretching for all joints.
Strengthening of the arms and any active muscles.
Breathing and cough training, especially in higher injuries.
Seated balance and transfer practice.
Standing with frames where appropriate.
exercises.howMuch: Daily, with regular review.
warnings: Pounding headache, sweating and flushing above the injury level in injuries at T6 or above. This can be autonomic dysreflexia and is an emergency.

faqs.q: What is autonomic dysreflexia?
faqs.a: A sudden rise in blood pressure triggered by things like a full bladder. It needs urgent action.

faqs.q: Can exercise help nerve recovery?
faqs.a: It supports whatever recovery is possible and maintains the body.

exercises.title: Sports Rehabilitation Exercises
exercises.summary: Sports rehabilitation exercises and return-to-sport programme. Phases, testing and injury prevention from Physiosolution sports physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Returning too early is a leading cause of re-injury. A structured plan builds the capacity your sport demands. Our physiotherapists use it most often for ACL tear, hamstring strain and ankle sprain, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Protect and restore: manage pain, restore range.
Build strength and control specific to the injured area.
Add power and agility: jumping, cutting, sprinting.
Sport-specific drills and gradual training return.
Testing: strength, hop tests and sport readiness.
exercises.howMuch: Daily rehab with training loads progressed weekly.
warnings: Pain or swelling increases with each progression.

faqs.q: How do I know I'm ready to return?
faqs.a: Meeting strength and function criteria, not just being pain-free.

faqs.q: Do you do injury prevention?
faqs.a: Yes, including warm-up and strength programmes.

exercises.title: Stair Training
exercises.summary: Stair training after stroke, knee or hip surgery. Safe technique, rail use and progression from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stairs require strength, balance and confidence. Learning the right sequence reduces effort and fall risk. Our physiotherapists use it most often for stroke, Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Hold the rail with the hand on the stronger side, or both rails if available.
Going up: step up with the stronger leg first, then the weaker leg, then the stick if used.
Going down: stick first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg.
One step at a time until strength improves.
Progress to step-over-step when safe.
exercises.howMuch: Practise daily on the stairs you use at home, with supervision at first.
warnings: You feel unsafe or have had a fall on stairs.

faqs.q: Up with the good, down with the bad?
faqs.a: The stronger leg lifts you up; the weaker leg leads down so the strong leg controls the lowering.

faqs.q: Can I manage stairs after a knee replacement?
faqs.a: Most people can before leaving hospital, one step at a time.

exercises.title: Standing and Walking Training
exercises.summary: Standing and walking training for children with developmental delay. Activities and equipment explained by Physiosolution pediatric physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Standing builds leg strength and bone health. Walking practice develops balance and coordination. Our physiotherapists use it most often for down syndrome, clubfoot and cerebral palsy, and it features in our pediatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Encourage pulling to stand at a low table with toys on it.
Cruising: move toys along the furniture so the child steps sideways.
Push toys: a stable push cart helps early walking.
Hand-held walking, reducing support gradually.
Orthoses or walkers may be prescribed for some children.
exercises.howMuch: Daily play, with therapy guidance.
warnings: Your child isn't walking by about 18 months, or walks on tiptoes consistently.

faqs.q: Are baby walkers helpful?
faqs.a: Seated baby walkers aren't recommended and can be unsafe.

faqs.q: When should a child walk?
faqs.a: Most walk between 9 and 18 months.

exercises.title: Step Downs
exercises.summary: Step down exercise for knee control, stairs and ACL rehab. Technique and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Going down stairs is harder on the knee than going up. Step downs build the control needed and correct inward knee collapse. Our physiotherapists use it most often for chondromalacia patella, ACL tear and total knee replacement, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand side-on on a low step, holding a rail.
Keep your weight on the leg on the step.
Slowly bend that knee to lower the other heel towards the floor.
Lightly tap the heel down, then straighten back up.
Watch in a mirror: the standing knee should stay over the second toe.
exercises.howMuch: 8 to 12 repetitions each leg, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Dropping quickly.
Hip hitching or knee collapsing inwards.
warnings: Kneecap pain limits the movement. Lower the step height.

faqs.q: Why does going downstairs hurt more?
faqs.a: The quadriceps work while lengthening, which puts higher load across the kneecap.

faqs.q: What step height should I use?
faqs.a: Start at 10 centimetres and progress to a standard stair.

exercises.title: Step Training
exercises.summary: Step training exercises for balance and fall prevention. Directions, speed progressions and safety from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: When balance is disturbed, a well timed step saves you. Practising steps in all directions trains that reaction. It is a regular part of rehab plans for Parkinson's disease, stroke and osteoporosis, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand next to a counter.
Step forward with one foot and return. Repeat with the other.
Step to the side, then backwards.
Progress to faster steps, or stepping to targets on the floor.
Advanced: step onto and off a low step.
exercises.howMuch: 10 steps in each direction with each leg, once a day.
warnings: You need to grab the support frequently. Slow down and ask for supervision.

faqs.q: How does this prevent falls?
faqs.a: It improves the speed and size of the step you take when you trip.

faqs.q: Can I do this alone?
faqs.a: If balance is reasonable and support is nearby. Otherwise, with someone present.

exercises.title: Step Ups
exercises.summary: Step up exercise for knee and hip strength. Correct technique, step height and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Step ups load one leg at a time through a functional range. Control of the knee over the foot is trained at the same time. You will often see it in our programmes for knee osteoarthritis, total knee replacement and ACL tear, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand facing a bottom stair or sturdy step, holding a rail if needed.
Place one whole foot on the step.
Push through that heel to step up, bringing the other foot up to join it.
Step down with the other leg first, slowly.
Keep the knee in line with the second toe throughout.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions each leg, 2 to 3 sets, once a day. Start with a low step (10 to 15 centimetres).
commonMistakes: Pushing off with the back foot instead of the leading leg.
Knee collapsing inwards.
warnings: Pain at the front of the knee increases after sessions.

faqs.q: How high should the step be?
faqs.a: Start low. Increase height once 3 sets feel easy and controlled.

faqs.q: Step ups or squats first?
faqs.a: Often squats, as both legs share the load. We decide based on your condition.

exercises.title: Straight Leg Raise
exercises.summary: Straight leg raise exercise for knee rehab. Technique, reps and progressions after knee surgery or injury, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Holding the knee straight while lifting trains the quadriceps to lock the knee, which is needed for walking without the knee buckling. It is a regular part of rehab plans for total knee replacement, ACL tear and meniscal injury, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lie on your back. Bend the other knee with the foot flat to protect your back.
Tighten the thigh muscle of the straight leg so the knee is fully straight.
Keeping it tight, lift the leg to the height of the other knee.
Hold 3 seconds and lower slowly.
Progress with an ankle weight.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Letting the knee bend as the leg lifts (a lag).
Lifting too high or too fast.
warnings: The knee cannot stay straight after several days of practice. We may need to work on activation first.

faqs.q: What is extensor lag?
faqs.a: When the knee bends as you lift, showing the quadriceps can't fully lock it yet.

faqs.q: Can I do this with a knee brace?
faqs.a: Yes, if your surgeon has fitted one and advised it.

exercises.title: Supported Squats
exercises.summary: Supported squats for older adults. Safe leg strengthening with a counter, reps and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Leg strength declines with age, making daily tasks harder. Squats reverse this with a movement that is easy to learn. It is a regular part of rehab plans for knee osteoarthritis, hip osteoarthritis and osteoporosis, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand facing a kitchen counter, holding it with both hands.
Feet hip width apart.
Bend your knees and push your hips back as if about to sit.
Go as low as is comfortable, then stand up tall.
Progress by holding on lightly with one hand.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions, 2 sets, once a day.
warnings: Knee or hip pain increases the next day.

faqs.q: How low should I go?
faqs.a: Only as low as feels comfortable and controlled.

faqs.q: Is squatting safe with arthritis?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Strengthening tends to reduce arthritis pain.

exercises.title: Tandem Walking
exercises.summary: Tandem walking and tandem standing (heel-to-toe) balance exercises. Progressions and safety from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: A narrow stance forces the ankles, hips and trunk to make small corrections, and relies on vision, inner ear and joint sensors working together. You will often see it in our programmes for Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and stroke, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Tandem stand: stand next to a counter and place one foot directly in front of the other, heel touching toe. Hold 30 seconds, then swap feet.
Tandem walk: walk along a counter or hallway, placing heel to toe with each step.
Look ahead, not at your feet, once steady.
Progress: hands off the support, then walking backwards heel to toe.
exercises.howMuch: Tandem stand 3 holds of 30 seconds. Tandem walk 3 to 4 lengths of 3 to 5 metres, once a day.
commonMistakes: Looking down constantly.
Rushing.
warnings: You feel dizzy or unsafe. Always practise with support within reach.

faqs.q: Is heel-to-toe walking the same exercise?
faqs.a: Yes. It's another name for tandem walking.

faqs.q: Why is it hard after a concussion?
faqs.a: Balance systems can be affected. Graded practice helps recovery.

exercises.title: Tendon Gliding Exercises
exercises.summary: Tendon gliding exercises for carpal tunnel syndrome and trigger finger. Five hand positions and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The flexor tendons pass through the carpal tunnel. Gliding them fully may reduce swelling around them and improve movement. Our physiotherapists use it most often for carpal tunnel syndrome, trigger finger and de Quervain's tenosynovitis, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Start with the fingers straight.
Hook fist: bend the top two finger joints, keeping the knuckles straight.
Full fist: bend all joints.
Table top: bend at the knuckles only, fingers straight.
Straight fist: bend the knuckles and middle joints, fingertips touching the palm base.
Return to straight between each. Hold each position 3 to 5 seconds.
exercises.howMuch: 5 to 10 cycles, 3 to 5 times a day.
commonMistakes: Rushing through positions.
Forcing painful triggering fingers.
warnings: Numbness is constant or thumb weakness develops in carpal tunnel syndrome.

faqs.q: Do these cure carpal tunnel?
faqs.a: They help mild cases alongside splinting and activity changes. Severe cases may need surgery.

faqs.q: My finger locks during the exercise. What now?
faqs.a: Avoid forcing it and get the finger assessed.

exercises.title: Terminal Knee Extension
exercises.summary: Terminal knee extension (TKE) exercise with a band. Technique and reps for ACL and knee replacement rehab from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: A knee that doesn't fully straighten makes walking tiring and loads the joint unevenly. TKE trains the quadriceps to lock the knee in standing. You will often see it in our programmes for ACL tear, total knee replacement and meniscal injury, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Loop a band around a sturdy object at knee height and step into it so it sits behind your knee.
Step back until the band is tight and the knee is slightly bent.
Straighten the knee fully against the band, squeezing the thigh.
Hold 2 to 3 seconds, then slowly let the knee bend again.
exercises.howMuch: 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Leaning the trunk back instead of straightening the knee.
Snapping the knee into hyperextension.
warnings: The knee won't reach straight after several weeks of rehab.

faqs.q: What if I don't have a band?
faqs.a: Pressing the back of the knee into a rolled towel while standing against a wall is an alternative.

faqs.q: Why is full straightening so important?
faqs.a: A persistently bent knee causes limping and extra joint load.

exercises.title: Thoracic Extension
exercises.summary: Thoracic extension exercise for upper back stiffness and posture. Chair and towel versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The thoracic spine should bend backwards and rotate freely. Hours of sitting round it forward. Extension restores movement and makes upright posture easier. It is a regular part of rehab plans for ankylosing spondylitis, scoliosis and cervical spondylosis, and it features in our upper back pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Chair version: sit in a chair with a backrest reaching mid-back. Support your head with your hands.
Gently lean back over the top of the backrest, then return upright.
Towel version: lie on your back with a firmly rolled towel across your upper back at shoulder blade level.
Support your head and let your upper back relax over the roll for 30 seconds.
Move the roll slightly higher or lower and repeat.
exercises.howMuch: 10 repetitions in the chair, or 3 positions on the towel, once or twice a day.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back instead of the upper back.
Letting the head drop backwards unsupported.
warnings: You have osteoporosis; avoid foam rollers and forceful extension unless guided.

faqs.q: Is a foam roller better than a towel?
faqs.a: It gives a stronger stretch. With osteoporosis or fragile ribs, a towel is safer.

faqs.q: Will this fix a hunchback?
faqs.a: It improves flexibility. Structural curves need assessment.

exercises.title: Toe Curls
exercises.summary: Toe curl and towel scrunch exercises for foot strength. How to do them and who benefits, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Strong toe flexors help grip the ground, support the arch and improve balance. It is a regular part of rehab plans for flat foot, metatarsalgia and hammer toe, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit with a towel flat on the floor under your foot.
Curl your toes to scrunch the towel towards you.
Relax and repeat until the towel is gathered.
Alternative: pick up small objects like marbles with your toes and drop them into a bowl.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 rounds, once a day.
commonMistakes: Using the ankle to drag the towel.
warnings: You have diabetes with numb feet. Check your skin afterwards for any marks.

faqs.q: Do toe curls help hammer toes?
faqs.a: They're often combined with toe stretches to maintain flexibility.

faqs.q: Short foot or toe curls?
faqs.a: Short foot targets the arch more specifically. Both have a place.

exercises.title: Toe Raises
exercises.summary: Toe raises for shin strength, foot drop and fall prevention. Technique and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The tibialis anterior lifts the foot as the leg swings through. Weakness causes the toes to catch, leading to trips. It is a regular part of rehab plans for ankle sprain, foot drop and diabetic neuropathy, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand with your back against a wall or hold a counter, heels close to the wall.
Keeping your heels on the floor, lift your toes and the front of your feet as high as possible.
Hold 2 seconds, then lower slowly.
Seated version: sit and lift the toes while keeping heels down.
exercises.howMuch: 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Leaning backwards or bending at the hips.
warnings: You notice new weakness in lifting the foot. It needs assessment for nerve causes.

faqs.q: Does this help foot drop?
faqs.a: It can help if some muscle activity is present. Complete foot drop may need a splint.

faqs.q: Should I do toe raises and heel raises together?
faqs.a: Yes, they balance each other.

exercises.title: Toe Walking
exercises.summary: Toe walking exercise for calf strength and ankle stability. Technique and precautions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Walking on tiptoes loads the calf and Achilles in a controlled way while training balance and foot muscle control. You will often see it in our programmes for achilles tendon rupture, ankle sprain and ankle instability, and it features in our sports physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Rise onto the balls of your feet near a wall or counter.
Walk forward in small steps, keeping the heels high.
Keep your posture upright.
Walk 10 metres, lower and rest.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 4 lengths, once a day, once standing calf raises are comfortable.
commonMistakes: Letting the heels drop as you tire.
Rolling onto the outer edge of the foot.
warnings: A child habitually walks on tiptoes. Persistent toe walking in children should be assessed rather than practised.

faqs.q: Is toe walking in children a problem?
faqs.a: Occasional toe walking in toddlers is common. Persistent toe walking past about age 3 should be checked.

faqs.q: When can I start after Achilles rupture?
faqs.a: Well into rehab, after strength is rebuilt. We guide timing.

exercises.title: Transfer Training
exercises.summary: Transfer training for stroke, spinal cord injury and elderly care. Safe bed-to-chair techniques and carer tips from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Transfers combine strength, balance and technique. Learning the right method reduces effort and the risk of falls for both patient and carer. You will often see it in our programmes for stroke, quadriplegia and motor neuron disease, and it features in our paralysis physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Set up: place the chair at a slight angle to the bed, brakes on if a wheelchair.
Shuffle forward to the edge, feet flat and slightly back.
Lean forward, push through the arms and legs to stand or lift.
Pivot on the feet towards the target seat.
Reach back for the armrest and sit slowly.
exercises.howMuch: Practise the transfers you need daily, with guidance until confident.
warnings: A carer is lifting most of your body weight. Equipment and technique changes may be needed.

faqs.q: Do you train family members?
faqs.a: Yes. Carer training is part of our home visits.

faqs.q: What equipment helps?
faqs.a: Transfer boards, grab rails and raised seats, depending on the person.

exercises.title: Triceps Stretch
exercises.summary: Triceps stretch for arm and shoulder flexibility. Technique and precautions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: It improves overhead reach by lengthening the triceps and the lower part of the shoulder capsule. Our physiotherapists use it most often for shoulder arthropathy, and it features in our shoulder pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Lift one arm overhead and bend the elbow so the hand reaches down your upper back.
Use the other hand to gently press the elbow back.
Keep your head up and back straight.
Hold 30 seconds, switch sides.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 holds each side, once a day.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back.
warnings: Overhead reach is painful. Work on shoulder range first.

faqs.q: Can I do this with frozen shoulder?
faqs.a: Only if you can lift the arm overhead comfortably.

faqs.q: Should I use a towel?
faqs.a: A towel behind the back can help if your hands can't reach.

exercises.title: Tummy Time
exercises.summary: Tummy time for babies. When to start, how long and how to make it easier, from Physiosolution pediatric physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Lifting the head against gravity builds the strength babies need for later milestones. Babies spend a lot of time on their backs for safe sleep, so awake tummy time balances this. It is a regular part of rehab plans for torticollis, down syndrome and Erb's palsy, and it features in our pediatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Start from the first weeks with a few minutes at a time, after a nappy change rather than straight after feeds.
Lie your baby on their tummy on a firm surface or on your chest.
Get down to their level and use toys, faces and voices to encourage them to lift their head.
A rolled towel under the chest can help if they find it hard.
Always stay with your baby.
exercises.howMuch: Build up gradually towards a total of around an hour a day across many short sessions by about 3 months.
warnings: Your baby always turns their head one way or has a flat spot. This may indicate torticollis.

faqs.q: My baby hates tummy time. What can I do?
faqs.a: Try short sessions, on your chest, or over your lap. It usually gets easier.

faqs.q: Can babies sleep on their tummy?
faqs.a: No. Sleep on the back; tummy time is for awake, supervised play.

exercises.title: Upper Trapezius Stretch
exercises.summary: Upper trapezius stretch for neck and shoulder tension. Correct technique, hold time and tips from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Stress, shrugging and poor workstation setup keep the upper trapezius switched on. Stretching it reduces the sense of tightness and can ease tension headaches. Our physiotherapists use it most often for cervical spondylosis, fibromyalgia syndrome and temporomandibular joint disorder, and it features in our neck pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit tall and hold the edge of the chair seat with your right hand to anchor the shoulder down.
Tilt your left ear towards your left shoulder.
Turn your nose slightly away from the stretched side if that increases the stretch.
Place your left hand lightly on your head to add a little weight, not force.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, then switch sides.
exercises.howMuch: 2 to 3 holds per side, 2 to 3 times a day.
commonMistakes: Letting the anchored shoulder rise.
Yanking the head with the hand.
warnings: The stretch causes tingling into the hand on either side.

faqs.q: Why do I get headaches with tight shoulders?
faqs.a: Tension in the upper trapezius and neck muscles can refer pain into the head. Stretching and posture changes often help.

faqs.q: Should I stretch or massage it?
faqs.a: Both can help. Stretching has the advantage of being something you can do several times a day.

faqs.q: What is the upper trapezius stretch?
faqs.a: The upper trapezius stretch tilts the ear towards one shoulder while the other shoulder stays down, stretching the top of the shoulder.

faqs.q: How is the upper trapezius stretch performed?
faqs.a: Sit upright and hold the edge of the chair seat with your right hand. This anchors the right shoulder down. Tilt your head to the left, bringing the left ear towards the left shoulder. For a deeper stretch, turn your nose slightly away from the right shoulder and rest your left hand lightly on your head. Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing slowly. You should feel a stretch along the right side of the neck towards the shoulder. Repeat 2 to 3 times on each side.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of the upper trapezius stretch?
faqs.a: It eases tight, sore shoulders and neck tension, especially from stress and computer work. It is often part of rehab for cervical spondylosis, fibromyalgia syndrome and temporomandibular joint disorder / TMJ.

faqs.q: Which muscles does the upper trapezius stretch target?
faqs.a: The upper trapezius, with some stretch of the scalenes.

exercises.title: Walking Exercises
exercises.summary: Walking exercise programme for seniors. How to start, progress and walk safely, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Regular walking maintains fitness and leg strength. In peripheral artery disease, supervised walking improves pain-free walking distance. You will often see it in our programmes for osteoporosis, peripheral artery disease and knee osteoarthritis, and it features in our geriatric physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Start with 5 to 10 minutes on flat ground at a comfortable pace.
Wear supportive shoes and use your walking aid if prescribed.
Add a few minutes every week.
Aim to walk at a pace where you can talk but not sing.
Choose safe, well lit routes; a mall or park path works well.
exercises.howMuch: Build up towards 30 minutes on most days, split into shorter walks if needed.
warnings: You get chest pain, severe breathlessness or dizziness.
Calf pain on walking limits you; it may be circulation-related.

faqs.q: Can walking replace other exercise?
faqs.a: It covers fitness well. Strength and balance exercises are also needed.

faqs.q: Is it okay to walk with knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Pace and distance can be adjusted.

exercises.title: Wall and Modified Push Ups
exercises.summary: Wall push-ups and modified push-ups for upper body strength and shoulder rehab. Progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Pushing exercises strengthen the chest, triceps and shoulder stabilisers, including the serratus anterior. Our physiotherapists use it most often for osteoporosis, shoulder impingement and rotator cuff injury, and it features in our shoulder pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Wall push-up: stand an arm's length from a wall, hands on it at shoulder height and width.
Bend the elbows to bring your chest towards the wall, keeping the body straight.
Push back out.
Progress to a counter or table, then to the floor from the knees, keeping a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Final stage: full push-ups.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, 3 days a week.
commonMistakes: Sagging hips.
Elbows flared straight out to the sides.
warnings: Pain at the front of the shoulder occurs.

faqs.q: What angle should elbows be at?
faqs.a: About 45 degrees from the body is kinder to the shoulders.

faqs.q: When can I do full push-ups?
faqs.a: When 3 sets of 15 knee push-ups are easy with good form.

exercises.title: Wall Slides
exercises.summary: Wall slides exercise for shoulder blade control and overhead shoulder pain. Technique and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The serratus anterior and lower trapezius rotate the shoulder blade as the arm lifts. When they are weak, the shoulder pinches overhead. Wall slides retrain that timing. It is a regular part of rehab plans for shoulder impingement, rotator cuff injury and supraspinatus tendinitis, and it features in our shoulder pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand facing a wall with your forearms on it, elbows at shoulder height and shoulder width apart.
Gently press your forearms into the wall so the shoulder blades wrap around the ribs.
Slide your forearms up the wall, keeping the pressure, until the arms are as high as comfortable.
Slowly slide back down.
Progress with a light band around the wrists, pushing outwards as you slide.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 12 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Shrugging as the arms rise.
Losing forearm contact with the wall.
Arching the back.
warnings: You feel pinching pain at the top of the shoulder that doesn't settle.

faqs.q: Is this the same as wall angels?
faqs.a: Similar idea. Wall angels are done with the back against the wall and are harder for stiff upper backs.

faqs.q: Can I do it with frozen shoulder?
faqs.a: Only once range allows. We usually start with assisted movements.

faqs.q: What are wall slides?
faqs.a: Wall slides move the forearms or hands up a wall while keeping the shoulder blades controlled.

faqs.q: How are wall slides performed?
faqs.a: Stand facing a wall with your forearms on it, elbows bent and about shoulder width apart, little fingers touching the wall. Gently press the forearms into the wall so the shoulder blades wrap around the ribs. Slide the forearms up the wall as far as you can without shrugging or arching your back. Slide back down slowly. Do 2 to 3 sets of 10.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of wall slides?
faqs.a: They improve overhead range, shoulder blade control and posture, and support rotator cuff rehab. They are often part of rehab for shoulder impingement, rotator cuff injury and supraspinatus tendinitis.

faqs.q: Which muscles do wall slides target?
faqs.a: The serratus anterior, lower trapezius and rotator cuff.

exercises.title: Wall Squats
exercises.summary: Wall squat (wall sit) for knee strength and patellar tendon pain. Depth, hold times and progressions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Isometric holds build strength and can reduce tendon pain in the short term, making wall squats useful in patellar tendinopathy. It is a regular part of rehab plans for patellar tendonitis, knee osteoarthritis and chondromalacia patella, and it features in our knee pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand with your back against a wall and feet about a foot in front of it, hip width apart.
Slide down the wall until your knees bend to a comfortable depth, no deeper than 90 degrees.
Keep knees over the ankles, not past the toes.
Hold for 10 to 45 seconds, then slide back up.
A ball between the knees helps keep alignment.
exercises.howMuch: 3 to 5 holds, once a day. For tendon pain, 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds are often used.
commonMistakes: Feet too close to the wall.
Going too deep too soon.
warnings: Kneecap pain increases during the hold. Reduce depth.

faqs.q: Why hold still rather than move?
faqs.a: Holding loads the muscle and tendon without repeated compression, which many sore knees prefer.

faqs.q: How deep for patellar tendon pain?
faqs.a: Usually 60 to 90 degrees knee bend, at a tolerable level. We set this.

exercises.title: Wall Walks
exercises.summary: Wall walks (finger ladder) for frozen shoulder and shoulder stiffness. How to do it and track progress, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Wall walking gives the arm partial support, so the shoulder can move higher than it can unaided. Marking the highest point lets you see progress week to week. You will often see it in our programmes for shoulder and arm fractures, shoulder arthropathy and rotator cuff injury, and it features in our frozen shoulder physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand facing a wall, about a forearm's length away.
Place your fingertips on the wall at waist height.
Walk your fingers up the wall slowly, stepping closer as needed.
Stop when you feel a stretch, hold 5 to 10 seconds, then walk back down.
Repeat side-on to the wall to work sideways lifting.
exercises.howMuch: 5 to 10 climbs, 2 to 3 times a day. Mark the highest point with a pencil or sticky note.
commonMistakes: Shrugging or leaning the body sideways to reach higher.
Arching the lower back.
warnings: Pain persists for more than an hour afterwards.

faqs.q: How fast should I see progress?
faqs.a: It varies. In frozen shoulder progress can be slow; small gains over weeks are normal.

faqs.q: Is it okay if it's uncomfortable?
faqs.a: A stretch is fine. Sharp pain is not.

faqs.q: What are wall walks?
faqs.a: Wall walks use the fingers to "walk" the hand up a wall, gradually lifting the arm higher.

faqs.q: How are wall walks performed?
faqs.a: Stand facing a wall about an arm's length away. Place your fingertips on the wall at waist height. Slowly walk your fingers up the wall, letting the arm rise with them. Step closer as you go if needed. Stop at a comfortable stretch, hold for 5 to 10 seconds, then walk the fingers back down. Repeat 5 to 10 times.

faqs.q: What are the benefits of wall walks?
faqs.a: They restore overhead reach after frozen shoulder, surgery or injury in a controlled, gradual way. They are often part of rehab for rotator cuff injury, shoulder arthropathy and shoulder and arm fractures.

faqs.q: Which muscles do wall walks target?
faqs.a: The deltoid and rotator cuff, while stretching the shoulder capsule.

exercises.title: Weight Bearing Exercises
exercises.summary: Weight bearing exercises for stroke, spinal cord injury and osteoporosis. Standing and supported loading from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Bone responds to load. Standing also stretches tight muscles and gives the brain feedback about body position. It is a regular part of rehab plans for stroke, cerebral palsy and spinal cord injury, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Supported standing: stand at a counter or in a standing frame for gradually longer periods.
Upper limb: lean on the affected arm with the hand flat on a table, elbow straight.
Weight shifts and mini squats once standing is steady.
Walking, as able, is the most useful weight bearing activity.
exercises.howMuch: Standing for 10 to 30 minutes daily where possible, built up gradually.
warnings: You have a recent fracture or restricted weight bearing after surgery.

faqs.q: What is a standing frame?
faqs.a: Equipment that supports someone who can't stand unaided.

faqs.q: Does weight bearing help osteoporosis?
faqs.a: Weight bearing and resistance exercise both support bone health.

exercises.title: Weight Shifting
exercises.summary: Weight shifting exercises for balance and walking recovery. How to do them after stroke or surgery, from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Walking is controlled weight transfer. Many people avoid putting weight through a weak or painful leg; shifting exercises rebuild that trust. You will often see it in our programmes for stroke, total knee replacement and total hip replacement, and it features in our neuro physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Stand with feet hip width apart, holding a counter.
Slowly shift your weight onto the right leg until the left feels light. Hold 5 seconds.
Shift to the left. Hold 5 seconds.
Repeat forwards and backwards with one foot slightly ahead.
Progress by reducing hand support.
exercises.howMuch: 10 shifts in each direction, 2 times a day.
warnings: After surgery, you haven't been cleared for full weight-bearing.

faqs.q: How do I know I'm putting enough weight through the weak leg?
faqs.a: Standing on two bathroom scales gives a simple check.

faqs.q: Is this useful after a stroke?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the first standing exercises.

exercises.title: Wrist Circles
exercises.summary: Wrist circles for wrist stiffness and warm-up. Technique and reps from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Combining all wrist movements keeps the small joints moving and increases blood flow before activity. You will often see it in our programmes for wrist fracture, carpal tunnel syndrome and de Quervain's tenosynovitis, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Rest your forearm on a table or hold it in front of you.
Make a loose fist or keep fingers relaxed.
Draw slow, large circles with your hand, 10 in each direction.
Keep the forearm still.
exercises.howMuch: 10 circles each way, several times a day.
commonMistakes: Moving the forearm instead of the wrist.
warnings: Clicking with pain or a clunk occurs on the little finger side of the wrist.

faqs.q: Can I do these at work?
faqs.a: Yes, they're ideal during typing breaks.

faqs.q: Do wrist circles help arthritis?
faqs.a: Gentle movement helps stiffness. Avoid pushing a hot, swollen joint.

exercises.title: Wrist Extensor Stretch
exercises.summary: Wrist extensor stretch for tennis elbow and forearm tightness. Technique and hold time from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The extensor muscles work with every grip. Stretching them relieves tightness and improves comfort during activity. It is a regular part of rehab plans for tennis elbow, de Quervain's tenosynovitis and radial tunnel syndrome, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Hold your arm straight in front with the palm facing down.
Bend the wrist so the fingers point to the floor.
Use the other hand to gently press the back of the hand towards you.
Hold 20 to 30 seconds. You should feel a stretch on the back of the forearm.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds, 2 to 3 times a day.
commonMistakes: Stretching into sharp elbow pain.
warnings: Elbow pain continues beyond several weeks despite activity changes.

faqs.q: Is stretching enough for tennis elbow?
faqs.a: Usually not. Progressive strengthening is the main treatment.

faqs.q: Can I stretch at my desk?
faqs.a: Yes, every hour or so during long typing sessions.

exercises.title: Wrist Flexion and Extension
exercises.summary: Wrist flexion and extension exercises for wrist fracture, tennis elbow and stiffness. Range and weighted versions from Physiosolution.
exercises.whatItDoes: Range exercises restore movement after immobilisation. Weighted versions strengthen the forearm muscles and tendons that attach at the elbow. It is a regular part of rehab plans for wrist fracture, smith fracture and forearm fractures, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Rest your forearm on a table with the hand over the edge, palm down.
Extension: lift the back of the hand up as far as comfortable, then lower slowly.
Turn the palm up. Flexion: curl the hand up, then lower slowly.
Once pain-free, hold a light weight or water bottle.
For tennis elbow, focus on slow lowering with the palm down.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, once a day.
commonMistakes: Lifting the forearm off the table.
Using a weight that is too heavy.
warnings: After a fracture, you haven't been cleared to start movement.

faqs.q: How soon after a wrist fracture can I start?
faqs.a: Usually once the cast is off, as advised by your doctor.

faqs.q: Why slow lowering for tennis elbow?
faqs.a: Controlled lengthening loads the tendon in a way that supports recovery.

exercises.title: Wrist Flexor Stretch
exercises.summary: Wrist flexor stretch for golfer's elbow and forearm tightness. Technique and hold times from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: The flexors work hard in gripping, lifting and racket sports. Stretching restores length and eases tension at the inner elbow. It is a regular part of rehab plans for Golfer's elbow, carpal tunnel syndrome and wrist fracture, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Hold your arm straight in front with the palm facing up.
Bend the wrist back so the fingers point to the floor.
Use the other hand to gently pull the fingers back towards you.
Hold 20 to 30 seconds.
exercises.howMuch: 3 holds, 2 to 3 times a day.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbow, which reduces the stretch.
warnings: Tingling develops in the little and ring fingers. It may be ulnar nerve irritation.

faqs.q: Why do I feel it in my fingers?
faqs.a: Some flexor muscles cross the fingers, so the stretch reaches them.

faqs.q: Does this help carpal tunnel?
faqs.a: Mild stretching may help some people. Avoid it if it increases tingling.

exercises.title: Wrist Pronation and Supination
exercises.summary: Pronation and supination exercises for forearm rotation after fractures. Assisted and hammer versions from Physiosolution physiotherapists.
exercises.whatItDoes: Rotation happens at joints near both the wrist and elbow, so fractures at either end can limit it. Repeated rotation restores range, and weighted versions build strength. Our physiotherapists use it most often for wrist fracture, forearm fractures and elbow fractures, and it features in our joint pain physiotherapy programmes.
steps: Sit with your elbow bent at 90 degrees, tucked against your side, forearm resting on a table.
Slowly turn your palm to face up, then down.
Hold 2 to 3 seconds at each end.
Progress by holding a hammer or bottle; the longer the lever, the harder it is.
exercises.howMuch: 10 to 15 repetitions, 2 to 3 sets, 2 to 3 times a day in early rehab.
commonMistakes: Moving the elbow away from the body to fake the rotation.
warnings: Rotation is not improving after several weeks following a fracture.

faqs.q: Why keep the elbow at my side?
faqs.a: It stops the shoulder from doing the work.

faqs.q: Which rotation matters most?
faqs.a: Supination is often more limited and needed for daily tasks.
